_README: Rich topics. The input to the Editorial Reel, and the replacement for the
hook+punchline pairs in topics.json.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
A topic in topics.json is about ten words. A thirty-second video needs
roughly eighty. generate-shorts.mjs closed that gap with filler, and in one
case with a number drawn at random from a pool and captioned 'Mind the
number.' A video about Nintendo's founding showed '5'. That is the failure
this file exists to make impossible: a topic either carries real content or
it does not get made into a video.
THE verified FLAG IS LOAD-BEARING
generate-reels.mjs refuses to emit props for a topic with verified:false
unless --allow-unverified is passed, and that flag also stamps the props so
the render is obviously a draft. Nothing unverified can reach a channel by
accident. Set verified:true only when every factual claim in the beats is
backed by an entry in sources, and you have actually read them.
ON NUMBERS SPECIFICALLY
A figure beat renders a value at 300px. That is an enormous claim to make.
Only add one where the number is real, specific and sourced. Most topics
below have no figure beat, because forcing one would mean inventing it, and
a four-beat video is the correct answer to not having a fifth true thing to
say. Being true is not enough either: a number that only two credible
sources disagree about, or that is an address, a duration or a count that
happens to exist, does not deserve to be the biggest thing on screen. Every
topic here that has no figure beat says in its verifiedNote which number was
considered and why it was cut. Read that before adding one back.
AND KEEP unit SHORT — IT CANNOT WRAP
FigureBeat lays the value and the unit out in one flex row with no wrap and
no shrink: 300px value, 22px gap, 76px unit, inside PAD=72 either side. That
leaves roughly 550px of unit for a two-digit value, which is about nine
characters. 'photoreceptors' was rendered and ran off the right edge with the
final s missing; it is 'receptors' now. Nothing warns about this — the only
way it shows up is rendering the reel and looking at it, so do that.
AND value MUST BE A WHOLE NUMBER
FigureBeat animates a count-up, and it derives the target with
parseInt(String(value).replace(/[^0-9]/g, '')). Every non-digit is deleted,
not parsed. '37.1' becomes the target 371 and renders as a giant 371. '1,300'
becomes 1300, '2.1' becomes 21. There is no warning and the props are valid;
you get a confidently wrong number at 300px, which is the exact failure this
file exists to prevent. Put the whole number in value and the precision in
context — tardigrade-heat shows 37 and says 37.1 underneath.
NO AMBIENT BED. THIS IS DELIBERATE.
The beds in public/sounds/ are synthesised from filtered noise. They were
normalised to fix a real problem (renders measured -43dB, silent on a phone)
and that made the wrong thing louder: amplified broad-spectrum noise reads as
radio static, not atmosphere. Four Reels shipped sounding like a broken radio
before anyone listened, because the check was a loudness measurement and not
an ear. Loud is not the same as good.
Silence is better than hiss. A Reel is watched muted more often than not, and
a clean silent video beats a noisy one. Narration still plays where a topic
has it. Do not restore a bed until there is real recorded ambience to use.
BEAT KINDS available: code, statement, credit, figure, kicker, sign.
Durations are NOT set here. generate-reels.mjs computes them from how long
each beat takes to animate and read, or from voiceCuts when a narration
track has been measured.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazuhisa_Hashimoto — Hashimoto (1958-2020) created the code while porting the arcade Gradius to the NES in 1986; he added a sequence granting full power-ups so he could finish the game for in-house testing, and intended to remove it before ship.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konami_Code — the game shipped with the code still in it; players found it and reported it back to Konami. Wider fame came with Contra in 1988, where the code granted additional lives.
https://www.npr.org/2020/02/26/809622331/kazuhisa-hashimoto-creator-of-famous-konami-code-gaming-cheat-dies — obituary confirming authorship and the Gradius origin.

https://contra.fandom.com/wiki/Konami_Code — the Contra figure specifically: the code gives 30 lives, shown in-game as 'Rest 30'. Corroborated by multiple cheat references; the code is commonly called the 30 Lives Code.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 11 Aug 2026. The '30 lives' figure was the one worth confirming separately from the origin story — Wikipedia says only 'additional lives', so the number comes from the Contra-specific sources. The beat text is left exactly as rendered because the narration track is cut to it; changing a word would desync voiceCuts.

beats.lead: But here is the part nobody says
beats.text: It was never meant to ship.
beats.note: The Konami Code was debug scaffolding. It was supposed to be deleted before release.

beats.name: Kazuhisa Hashimoto
beats.role: Porting Gradius to the NES. He could not get through his own game well enough to test it, so he wrote a shortcut that handed the player every power-up at once.

beats.context: What the same code granted in Contra, two years later. That is the version most people remember.

beats.text: He forgot to take it out.

beats.line: A bug that outlived the console.

sources: https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_334663 — the Smithsonian National Museum of American History's own catalogue entry for the log book with the moth still taped in.
https://www.computerhistory.org/tdih/september/9/ — date and machine: 9 September 1947, Harvard Mark II.

https://daily.jstor.org/the-bug-in-the-computer-bug-story/ — the correction that matters: 'bug' for a technical fault predates 1947 by over a century, back to Edison, so this was never the coining of the term.

https://www.pricefx.com/learning-center/software-engineering-debacles-grace-hopper-and-the-first-reported-bug — the logbook wording: '15:45 Relay #70 Panel F (moth) in relay. First actual case of bug being found.'
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 11 Aug 2026. Grace Hopper is deliberately NOT named. Sources agree she was on the Mark II team and popularised the story in later lectures, but the log book was probably not hers and the attribution is contested. The beats credit the machine and an unnamed operator instead, which is what the evidence actually supports. The joke in the note beat — that engineers had used 'bug' for decades before one turned out to be literal — is the JSTOR correction, used as the hook rather than buried. There WAS a figure beat here showing 70, the relay number, and it was cut. The number is true and sourced, but a figure beat renders its value at 300px, and the relay number carries no significance whatsoever — it is an address, not a fact. Setting it that large would have overstated it. Being true is not sufficient; a number given that much emphasis has to deserve it. The detail now sits in a statement beat where it reads as the log entry it actually is.

beats.lead: The word is older than the machine
beats.text: One day the bug was literal.
beats.note: Engineers had called faults bugs since Edison. On this one afternoon, someone opened a relay and found an actual insect.

beats.name: Harvard Mark II
beats.role: 9 September. An operator traced a fault to a moth caught in a relay, removed it, and taped it into the log book instead of throwing it away.

beats.lead: What they wrote in the log
beats.text: First actual case of bug being found.
beats.note: Relay #70, Panel F. 15:45. The wording gives it away — they knew the joke they were making.

beats.text: They kept the moth.

beats.line: It is still taped to the page, in the Smithsonian.

topics.verifiedNote: Checked 11 Aug 2026. Tim Mott is credited alongside Tesler in every source, so the credit beat names both — 'invented by Larry Tesler' alone is the popular shorthand and it is not quite right. No figure beat: there is no real number here, and a usage statistic would have had to be invented, which is the exact thing this file exists to prevent. beats.role: At Xerox PARC they built a text editor called Gypsy, where selecting text and moving it worked the same way every time, with no hidden mode to remember first.

beats.text: In 1975 it turned up in Businessweek.

sources: https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/a-different-form-of-color-vision-in-mantis-shrimp/ — the institutional record of the paper, carrying the full Science abstract: Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall, 'A different form of color vision in mantis shrimp', Science 343(6169):411-413, 24 Jan 2014, PMID 24458639. Establishes the 12 photoreceptor types sampling 300-720nm, that three or four are sufficient for fine colour discrimination, the 'surprisingly poor' behavioural wavelength discrimination, and the temporal-scanning recognition hypothesis.

https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/the-mantis-shrimp-sees-like-a-satellite — Ed Yong's report from the week of publication. Source for the discrimination numbers actually put on screen: humans separate wavelengths about 5nm apart, the shrimp only 15-25nm. Also the species tested (Haptosquilla trispinosa), the training method, and Justin Marshall's own framing — 'Actually, they're much worse!' and the satellite lookup-table comparison.
https://www.calacademy.org/explore-science/mantis-shrimp-vision — California Academy of Sciences, checked as a third institutional statement of the same finding.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. The figure beat is 12 and it earns the 300px: the entire popular myth is built on that number, so the video's turn only works if the number is the biggest thing on screen first. Note that this batch also contains vanilla-albius, whose emotional core is a twelve-year-old — that topic was deliberately given NO figure beat rather than a second giant '12' on the same channel. Do not 'improve' it by adding one back. Deliberately not said: any claim about how many colours the animal sees. Sources agree on receptor count, not on any colour count, and '100,000 colours' style figures are invented. The 8-visible/4-UV split comes from Yong; the abstract only gives the 300-720nm range, so the split is stated as description rather than as the headline number. The unit reads 'receptors' and not 'photoreceptors' for a layout reason, not a factual one: the first render clipped 'photoreceptors' off the right edge of the frame, because FigureBeat puts the unit on one unwrapped line beside a 300px number. Do not lengthen it back. 'You manage five' is the human 5nm discrimination threshold from Yong, rounded as he gives it. The mechanism beat says 'may not compare colours at all' rather than asserting it — the paper itself says 'suggest', and Marshall's own quoted answer to what they do instead was 'Dunno'. ADDENDUM, 1 Sep 2026: added a media beat at the very front, opening the video on the actual animal (assets/bg/mantis-shrimp-colour-demo.mp4, reviewed and cleared in scripts/data/animate-imagery-review.json — real footage, eyes cropped out of frame per the standing content rule) instead of opening cold on type. Its caption is the existing lead line reused verbatim, not new copy, and none of the six original beats below were touched: same wording, same order, same facts. This addendum documents the addition; it does not reopen or restate the fact-checking above.

beats.lead: The internet's favourite animal fact
beats.text: It is not what you were told.
beats.note: The mantis shrimp is famous for seeing colours you cannot imagine. In 2014 someone tested what it can actually tell apart.

beats.context: Eight across the range you can see, four more in the ultraviolet. You have three. Four is already enough for fine colour discrimination.

beats.lead: Then they ran the test
beats.text: It is worse at this than you are.
beats.note: It could only separate wavelengths fifteen to twenty-five nanometres apart. You manage five. So do honeybees.

beats.name: Hanne Thoen
beats.role: Working in Justin Marshall's lab in Queensland, she found the eye may not compare colours at all. It scans, and matches the reading against something like a lookup table.

beats.text: It is not seeing more. It is seeing faster.

beats.line: The best-known fact about this animal is the wrong one.

sources: https://www.eso.org/public/news/eso2109/ — ESO's release on Montargès et al., Nature, 16 June 2021. Establishes the dimming through late 2019 and early 2020, the VLT images, and that the star was partially concealed by a cloud of dust.

https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/news/mystery-solved-dust-cloud-led-betelgeuses-great-dimming — Harvard & Smithsonian CfA, same date, independent institution. Source for 'lost more than two-thirds of its brightness', the January and March 2020 images, the mechanism (ejected gas bubble, a patch of surface cooled, heavier elements such as silicon condensed into dust), the return to normal brightness by April 2020, and Montargès' line about watching a star's appearance change in real time on a scale of weeks.

https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/hubble-finds-that-betelgeuses-mysterious-dimming-is-due-to-a-traumatic-outburst/ — Dupree's earlier Hubble work, reaching the dust conclusion by a different route and independently.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.05982 — the dissent, read and deliberately accounted for: 'The Photospheric Temperatures of Betelgeuse during the Great Dimming of 2019/2020: No New Dust Required'.
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-25018-3 — 'Spectroscopic evidence for a large spot on the dimming Betelgeuse', the competing large-cool-spot emphasis.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, on purpose. The candidates were the V-band magnitude at minimum (1.6, jargon that means nothing at 300px), the fraction of light lost (given variously as 'more than two-thirds', '70%' and '1.2 magnitudes' — approximate, and stated differently by each source), and 200,000 mph for the ejected material (single-sourced to Dupree). None of them is both crisp and load-bearing, so the topic runs on the correction instead. The dust explanation is stated as the answer astronomers arrived at, which is what ESO, CfA and NASA all say — but the exact mechanism is genuinely still argued, with at least one paper titled 'No New Dust Required' and another pushing a large cool spot. The beat wording follows CfA's version (gas ejected, surface patch cools, silicon condenses) because that account is compatible with the cool-spot camp rather than opposed to it. Do not upgrade 'the answer came' to 'proven'. Also deliberately not said: the distance to Betelgeuse, and any timescale for the supernova. Both are quoted with enormous error bars and neither survives being set in type.

beats.lead: Late in 2019 a star started going out
beats.text: The headlines said supernova.
beats.note: Betelgeuse, the orange shoulder of Orion, lost more than two thirds of its light by February 2020. Then it came back.

beats.name: Betelgeuse
beats.role: A red supergiant close enough that a telescope can resolve its actual surface. Between January and March, astronomers watched the southern half of it darken, week by week.

beats.lead: The answer, June 2021
beats.text: It was dust.
beats.note: The star threw off a bubble of gas. A patch of surface behind it cooled, silicon condensed, and it hid behind its own soot.

beats.text: It will explode. That was not it.

beats.line: Still there. Still the shoulder of Orion.

sources: https://www.linnean.org/news/2019/10/16/edmond-albius — the Linnean Society's account, which quotes Ferréol Bellier-Beaumont's own 1861 letter to the Justice of the Peace at Sainte-Suzanne ('I taught the little black boy, Edmond, how to marry the male and female parts together... This clever boy had realized that the vanilla flower also had male and female elements'), his rebuttal of Jean Michel Claude Richard's counter-claim ('How could Mr. Richard have taught the young boy this technique in 1838 — when he was only eight years old?'), the 20-year-old barren vine, the 1880 Moniteur death notice, and Arditti et al. 2009's conclusion that the discovery was Albius's own.

https://www.europeana.eu/en/stories/edmond-albius — Europeana, story contributed by the Fondation pour la Mémoire de l'Esclavage. Independently gives birth at Sainte-Suzanne on 9 August 1829, the 1841 discovery at twelve, freedom in 1848, death in poverty in 1880, and that the hand-pollination method is still used worldwide.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Albius — checked only to confirm the age at discovery agrees with the two above.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, and the reason is editorial rather than factual: his age is well sourced and would have made a strong 300px '12', but mantis-shrimp-colour in this same batch already puts a giant 12 on the same channel, and two videos opening on the same numeral would read as a template. The age is carried in the credit beat instead. If mantis-shrimp-colour is ever retired, this is the topic that should get the figure beat back. Deliberately left out: all tonnage figures. The Linnean Society gives Réunion exports as 2 tonnes in 1858, 20 in 1867, 200 in 1898; Europeana gives about 1 tonne a year in the 1850s, 15 in the following decade, 60 by the early 1880s. Those do not reconcile, so no export number appears anywhere. Also left out: what crop gave him the idea. Bellier-Beaumont's own letter says watermelon, Europeana says pumpkin, and rather than pick one the beat now just says he worked it out himself. Deliberately included, because it is the actual correction: Albius was not the first to hand-pollinate vanilla — Charles Morren published the technique in 1837, four years earlier — but Morren's method suited a greenhouse and not a plantation. The beats therefore never say he was first, only that the method that scaled was his. Do not add 'invented'.

beats.lead: Almost every vanilla pod you have eaten
beats.text: Was pollinated by hand.
beats.note: The orchid has its own bee only in Mexico. Everywhere else someone opens each flower and does it themselves, one at a time.

beats.name: Edmond Albius
beats.role: Twelve, born into slavery on Réunion and taught horticulture by the man who owned him. He saw the flower's two halves were separated by a flap you could lift.

beats.lead: His owner did not believe it
beats.text: Then more pods appeared.
beats.note: Bellier-Beaumont had kept one barren vine alive twenty years. In 1861 he wrote that the boy worked it out himself.

beats.lead: Others claimed it
beats.text: He said he taught the boy.
beats.note: Bellier-Beaumont checked the dates: by that account Edmond was eight. Archivists went back over it in 2009 and agreed it was his.

beats.text: He died in a public hospital with nothing.

beats.line: The method has not changed since.

sources: https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/1816-the-year-without-summer.htm — US National Park Service. Source for the Tambora attribution, the nicknames ('Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death'), and every weather detail on screen: May frost killing crops in New York, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Vermont; June snow at Albany, New York and Dennysville, Maine; lakes and rivers still frozen in July as far south as north-western Pennsylvania.

https://www.gutenberg.org/files/42324/42324-h/42324-h.htm — Project Gutenberg's text of the 1831 Frankenstein, where Mary Shelley's own author's introduction gives the quoted words: 'it proved a wet, ungenial summer, and incessant rain often confined us for days to the house.'
https://www.britannica.com/event/Haunted-Summer-of-1816 — Britannica on the Villa Diodati party (Byron, Percy and Mary, Claire Clairmont, Polidori) and the ghost-story agreement.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer — checked for the global temperature anomaly, which is why no temperature figure appears here.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, and no temperature anywhere. The NPS says the cloud 'changed the global climate by 2-7 degrees Fahrenheit'; Wikipedia gives the global average anomaly as 0.4-0.7°C, which is about 0.7-1.3°F. Those are different claims — one is almost certainly regional and the other a global mean — and putting either at 300px would be asserting a precision the sources do not share. The causal chain is deliberately only half-drawn. Tambora causing the cold is stated, because NPS states it directly. Tambora causing Frankenstein is NOT stated: the beats put the party indoors in the rain and quote Mary Shelley's own account of why, and stop there. 'A volcano wrote Frankenstein' was drafted as the kicker and cut, because it is the sort of tidy line that is repeated until it becomes a fact. The kicker used instead — that nobody in the room knew why it was raining — is the true and better point. Also note 1816 was already sitting on a cold decade and there was an earlier unidentified eruption around 1808-09, so Tambora is the trigger rather than the whole explanation; the credit beat says it 'put enough into the stratosphere to shade the planet', which is what the source supports, and not 'caused'.

beats.lead: In 1816 the summer did not arrive
beats.text: It snowed in June.
beats.note: May frost killed the crops across New England. June snow fell on Albany. In July there was still ice on Pennsylvania rivers.

beats.name: Mount Tambora
beats.role: An Indonesian volcano had erupted the year before and put enough into the stratosphere to shade the planet. Nobody in New England made the connection.

beats.lead: That June on Lake Geneva
beats.text: It rained for days.
beats.note: Byron, the Shelleys and Polidori were shut inside a rented villa. To fill the evenings they each agreed to write a ghost story.

beats.lead: Mary Shelley, writing in 1831
beats.text: A wet, ungenial summer.
beats.note: Her words: incessant rain often confined us for days to the house. She was eighteen. What she started that week was Frankenstein.

beats.text: Nobody in that room knew why.

beats.line: They called it eighteen hundred and froze to death.

sources: https://core.tdar.org/project/459204/atari-dump-site-alamogordo-new-mexico-usa — the Digital Archaeological Record's project entry, the primary archaeological record (project director Andrew Reinhard, field director Richard Rothaus, PI Joe Lewandowski; doi:10.48512/XCV8459204). Establishes the September 1983 deposit, that it was reported at the time in the New York Times and the Alamogordo Daily News before becoming an urban legend, the 26 April 2014 excavation by the City of Alamogordo with archaeologists and a film crew, 'recovered just over 1,300 games', the 10-metre depth, the manifest as the most important result, and the receiving institutions: the Smithsonian, the Tularosa Basin Historical Museum, The Strong National Museum of Play, the Henry Ford, and VIGAMUS in Rome.

https://www.thehenryford.org/collections/explore/artifact/403653 — the Henry Ford's own catalogue entry for an excavated E.T. cartridge (object ID 2015.13.15, gift of the City of Alamogordo), independently confirming the 26 April 2014 date and that the material is now museum-accessioned.
https://archaeology.org/issues/july-august-2014/digs-discoveries/new-mexico-atari-dump-site-excavation/ — Archaeology Magazine's contemporaneous write-up of the dig.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, and the count of buried cartridges is deliberately absent from every beat. tDAR says 'ca. 800,000'; the Henry Ford says 700,000. Both are credible primary-adjacent institutions and they do not agree, so the beats say 'hundreds of thousands' and nothing more precise. The recovered count is given as 'just over 1,300' — tDAR's own wording — rather than the 1,382 that circulates in press coverage, because tDAR is the excavation's own record and the press figure could not be traced to it. A figure beat was drafted twice and cut twice: first with the buried count (contested, see above), then with 31, the years between burial and dig. 31 is true and arithmetic from two solid dates, but it is a duration, and a duration at 300px implies a significance it does not have. The story is the myth turning out to be documented, not any one number. Also not said: that concrete was poured over the cell. It is repeated everywhere and appears in none of the three sources read here.

beats.lead: For thirty years this was a rumour
beats.text: Atari buried its games in the desert.
beats.note: September 1983: trucks took hundreds of thousands of cartridges out to a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico, and buried them.

beats.name: Alamogordo, New Mexico
beats.role: The New York Times reported it at the time. Then it slid out of the record and became a story gamers told each other, always about E.T.

beats.lead: On 26 April 2014 they dug
beats.text: All of it was true.
beats.note: The city, archaeologists and a film crew went ten metres down and pulled up just over 1,300 cartridges. Not only E.T.

beats.lead: Where the finds went
beats.text: The Smithsonian took some.
beats.note: So did the Henry Ford, the Strong Museum of Play and the video game museum in Rome. A landfill became a catalogued site.

beats.text: The urban legend had a manifest.

beats.line: Some myths are only undocumented.

sources: http://kanji.zinbun.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~yasuoka/publications/PreQWERTY.html — Koichi Yasuoka and Motoko Yasuoka, 'On the Prehistory of QWERTY', ZINBUN No.42 (March 2011), pp.161-174, with the authors' own abstract. The 'to slow down the operator' answer is quoted there and called, in their word, nonsense. Also the derivation from the Hughes-Phelps printing telegraph, the development for Morse receivers, and that the arrangement changed repeatedly and 'accidentally grew into QWERTY'.

https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-qwerty-keyboard-will-never-die-where-did-the-150-year-old-design-come-from-49863249/ — Smithsonian Magazine, quoting the paper directly for the Morse detail used on screen: American Morse renders Z as '... .', easily confused with the digram SE, so S needed to sit near both Z and E. Also Sholes' 1868 typewriter patent, and his 1889 application for an XPMCH layout filed a year before his death.

https://oztypewriter.blogspot.com/2012/10/on-this-day-in-typewriter-history-from.html — independent confirmation of the two dates put on screen: Sholes applied for design 568,630 in September 1889 and died at Milwaukee on 17 February 1890, the patent being assigned after his death.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Christopher-Latham-Sholes — checked for Sholes' dates (1819-1890).
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat: the available numbers are the 1874 price of $125, and Remington's 1891 claim of 100,000 machines in use. Both are true and both are beside the point, which is that the reason everyone gives for the layout is wrong. The Morse Z/SE claim is the Yasuokas' argument, not an independently established fact, and the beat is worded to attribute it — 'their evidence' — rather than to state it as settled. It is worth knowing that the jamming account is not universally abandoned; Smithsonian describes it as contentious rather than dead, so the beats say the researchers who traced the history called it nonsense, which is precisely what happened, instead of saying it has been disproved. The code beat carries QWERTYUIOP rather than QWERTY because the ten-glyph top row is what a viewer recognises on sight and it gives the CodeBeat stagger enough to work with. The kicker is the real find: the man who gave us the layout filed a patent for a different one in September 1889 and was dead by the following February, so he spent his last months trying to replace it.

beats.caption: You have never once questioned this.

beats.lead: What everyone says
beats.text: It was built to slow you down.
beats.note: So the typebars would not jam. It is in textbooks. The researchers who traced the layout's real history called that, in print, nonsense.

beats.name: Koichi and Motoko Yasuoka
beats.role: At Kyoto University they followed the keyboard back past the typewriter to the telegraph. Its first heavy users were Morse operators taking down code live.

beats.lead: Their evidence
beats.text: American Morse writes Z almost like S-E.
beats.note: An operator could not tell them apart until the following letters arrived. So S ended up next to both Z and E.

beats.text: Sholes spent his last year trying to replace it.

beats.line: You are typing on his rough draft.

sources: https://doi.org/10.1091/mbc.E16-07-0509 — Michael W. topics.verifiedNote: Checked 17 Aug 2026. NO figure beat: the mint numbers only mean anything as a pair — 440 million falling to 292 million — and a lone giant number would assert nothing. sources: https://sites.google.com/view/elizagen-org/blog/eliza-reanimated — the restoration team's own account (Rupert Lane, Anthony Hay, Arthur Schwarz, Jeff Shrager): ELIZA created by Weizenbaum at MIT 1964-6; ELIZA uses a script to determine its personality; David Berry suggested the code might be in Weizenbaum's papers, and in 2021 Shrager worked with MIT archivist Myles Crowley to find, in a folder dated 1965, a printout of the source alongside two early drafts of the DOCTOR script; the code is 53 pages, around 2,600 lines, mostly uncommented; it did not OCR well so Hay and Schwarz hand-transcribed it; three functions were missing and replacements were written, leaving 96% of the source from the original files; run on Dave Pitts's IBM 7094 emulator with CTSS; it nearly exactly recreated the 'Men are all alike' conversation from the 1966 CACM paper.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELIZA — ELIZA written in MAD-SLIP for CTSS on an IBM 7094; SLIP is Weizenbaum's own Symmetric LIst Processor; DOCTOR was the most famous script and the only one published; named after Eliza Doolittle in Shaw's Pygmalion because the program could be incrementally improved; Weizenbaum's secretary asked him to leave the room so she and ELIZA could talk, and he wrote in Computer Power and Human Reason (1976, p. 7) that he 'had not realized ... that extremely short exposures to a relatively simple computer program could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people'; the source was missing from the 1960s until the 2021 MIT archive find; December 2024 for the reanimation.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 18 Aug 2026. The figure beat is 96 and it earns the 300px: the whole claim of the restoration is that this is Weizenbaum's code running, not a reimplementation of it, and the percentage is the restorers' own accounting. Candidates cut: 2,600 (lines) and 53 (pages) are specs, not facts that carry the story, and both live in the figure's context instead; 56 (years lost) is a duration. Deliberately not said: that ELIZA 'passed the Turing test' — it did not, and Weizenbaum said in Plug & Pray that only people who misunderstood it called it a sensation. The 2023 preprint in which ELIZA outscored GPT-3.5 in a Turing-test study is left out because it is a single unrefereed result and would imply the opposite of the point. The secretary is not named because neither source names her. 1966 is used in the credit beat as the publication year of the CACM paper; the program itself was built across 1964-66 and the recovered printout is dated 1965, which is why the beats say built and published rather than giving one date for both.

beats.lead: The first chatbot was not a therapist
beats.text: The therapist was a script.
beats.note: ELIZA was the program: find a keyword, take the sentence apart, put it back together as a question. DOCTOR was one script it could load. Load a different script and the psychotherapist is simply gone.

beats.name: Joseph Weizenbaum
beats.role: Built at MIT in MAD-SLIP, a list-processing language he had written himself, on an IBM 7094 shared with around thirty other users. He named it after Eliza Doolittle, who could be taught to speak.

beats.lead: His own secretary had watched him build it
beats.text: She asked him to leave the room.
beats.note: She wanted to talk to it alone. He wrote afterwards that he had not realised extremely short exposures to a relatively simple program could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people.

beats.lead: Then the code was gone
beats.text: Nobody published source in 1966.
beats.note: It stayed missing for decades. In 2021 Jeff Shrager and the MIT archivist Myles Crowley opened a folder in Weizenbaum's papers marked Computer Conversations and found the printout, with two draft DOCTOR scripts beside it.

beats.context: That much of what runs today is Weizenbaum's own code. Fifty-three pages would not scan, so it was retyped by hand; three missing functions were rewritten; the rest compiled on an emulated 7094.

beats.line: In 2024 it answered again, and said what it said in 1966.

sources: https://www.nintendo.com/en-gb/Iwata-Asks/Iwata-Asks-New-Super-Mario-Bros-Wii/Volume-1/2-The-Reason-Mario-Wears-Overalls/2-The-Reason-Mario-Wears-Overalls-210759.html — Iwata Asks, Miyamoto in his own words: the original Mario was a 16x16 pixellated image; overseas games drew human figures six or eight heads tall, which at that size left only a couple of pixels for the face; he drew the character himself because he was convinced those figures had been drawn by programmers who could not draw; 'if you draw a nose then a moustache, you don't really know if it's a mouth or a moustache, and it saves pixels'; 'you don't have to draw a mouth, which makes a big difference'; one pixel for the chin, two vertical pixels for eyes; 'because you can't fully draw hair, by making him wear a hat, you can reduce the hair to only a couple of pixels', and hair 'presents problems to animate'; only three frames were available for the run, so to make the arm movement easier to see the arms and body needed different colours, which is why he wears overalls; white gloves were added to make his movements easier to spot when he jumped; the game was set on a construction site so they made him a carpenter; Miyamoto called him 'Mr. Video' and someone at Nintendo of America came up with the name Mario.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 18 Aug 2026. The figure beat is 3 and it earns the 300px because it is causal rather than decorative: three run frames is the constraint that produced the overalls, which is the one design decision here that outlived the hardware by forty years. Candidates cut: 16 (the sprite was 16x16, so a lone 16 at that size would be a confidently wrong number of exactly the kind the _README warns about) and 8 (the 8x8 pixel budget for the face, which is a spec). This is Donkey Kong's Mario, not Super Mario Bros. — the interview's construction site, carpenter and Jumpman all place it there, and the beats never say Super Mario Bros. The year 1981 in the credit beat is Donkey Kong's release, which the source implies but does not state; nothing else in the entry depends on it. Deliberately not said: 'Mario is an Italian plumber' — Miyamoto says carpenter and a construction site, the plumbing came later, and the naming is credited to Nintendo of America, not to him. The clouds-and-bushes palette swap is a real and separate Super Mario Bros. fact from a different interview and is left for its own topic rather than blended in here.

beats.lead: The moustache is not characterisation
beats.text: It is there so they could skip the mouth.
beats.note: Miyamoto's reasoning: draw a nose and then a moustache, and nobody can tell whether the thing underneath is a mouth or a moustache. So you never draw one. At sixteen pixels across, that saving was worth having.

beats.name: Shigeru Miyamoto
beats.role: He drew the character himself. Imported games rendered people six or eight heads tall, which left two pixels for a face, and he was convinced those figures had been drawn by programmers rather than by anyone who could draw.

beats.lead: The cap solves two problems at once
beats.text: Hair will not fit, and will not move.
beats.note: There were not enough pixels for hair, and animating it was worse. A hat cut hair down to a couple of pixels and let him set the eyes directly underneath, which finished the face.

beats.context: That is everything he had for a run. To make the arm swing readable at that speed, the arms had to be a different colour from the body — so Mario got overalls. The white gloves came next, to find his hands mid-jump.

beats.text: Miyamoto wanted to call him Mr. Video.

beats.line: Someone at Nintendo of America named him Mario.

sources: https://scottbarrykaufman.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/Macnamara-et-al.-2014.pdf — Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, 'Deliberate Practice and Performance in Music, Games, Sports, Education, and Professions: A Meta-Analysis', Psychological Science 25, 1608-1618. Read directly. Describes Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Romer (1993) as recruiting musicians of differing accomplishment and asking them to ESTIMATE their deliberate practice per week for each year of their lives; states that at age 20 the average for the 'best' violinists was more than 10,000 hr, about 7,800 hr for the 'good' violinists and about 4,600 hr for the least-accomplished group; names Gladwell's Outliers (2008) as the inspiration for the '10,000-hour rule — the idea that it takes 10,000 hr of practice to become an expert'; reports deliberate practice explaining 26% of the variance for games, 21% for music, 18% for sports, 4% for education and less than 1% for professions; and, in the moderator analysis, that for studies using the log method — 'which presumably yields more valid estimates than retrospective methods do' — deliberate practice accounted for only 5% of the variance in performance. Concludes 'deliberate practice is important, but not as important as has been argued.'
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 18 Aug 2026. The figure beat is 5 and it earns the 300px because it is the finding that actually moves the argument: the effect size depends on whether the practice was logged or remembered, and the rule descends entirely from remembered hours. Candidates cut: 10,000 (it is the popular claim being corrected, and setting it enormous would restate the myth), 26 (the largest domain figure, but quoting the best number as the headline is the same selective reading the entry criticises) and 1993 (a date). All hour figures are the age-20 averages as reported in Macnamara et al.; other by-age-18 figures for the same study circulate widely (7,410 / 5,301 / 3,420) and are NOT used here, because they were not read in a source and mixing the two ages is how the numbers get garbled. Deliberately not said: that half the best violinists fell below 10,000 hours — it follows only if the distribution is symmetric, which no source read here reports. Also not said: that practice does not matter, or anything about innate talent; the paper's own conclusion is that deliberate practice is important but not as important as argued, and the entry stops there. Ericsson's personal objections to Gladwell are real and widely quoted, but no source stating them was read in full, so no beat attributes a view to him.

beats.lead: Nobody ever found a ten-thousand-hour threshold
beats.text: It was an average, at one music school.
beats.note: Violinists in Berlin, sorted by how good their teachers thought they were. By age twenty the best group averaged over 10,000 hours, the good group about 7,800, the least accomplished about 4,600. A gradient, not a gate.

beats.name: Malcolm Gladwell
beats.role: Outliers turned that gradient into the ten-thousand-hour rule — the idea that ten thousand hours of practice makes an expert. The 1993 paper it came from does not say so anywhere.

beats.lead: And the hours were never counted
beats.text: They were remembered.
beats.note: Each musician was asked to estimate how much they had practised per week, for every year of their life, looking backwards. Every hour in the study is a recollection of an hour.

beats.context: In a 2014 meta-analysis, that is all the variance in performance deliberate practice explained — once you restrict it to the studies that logged practice as it happened instead of asking people to recall it.

beats.lead: Pooled across every field they could find
beats.text: The number moves with the room.
beats.note: Practice explained 26 percent of the variance in games, 21 in music, 18 in sports, 4 in education, and under 1 percent in the professions. Their own summary: important, but not as important as has been argued.

beats.line: The rule is somebody else's average, rounded.

sources: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/neat-and-tidy-map-tastes-tongue-you-learned-school-all-wrong-180963407/ — Steven D. Munger (Director, University of Florida Center for Smell and Taste) with Drew Wilson, republished from The Conversation. Establishes: the map's root is D. P. Hanig's 1901 'Zur Psychophysik des Geschmackssinnes'; Hanig measured thresholds around the edges of the tongue — what he called the taste belt — by dripping salty, sweet, sour and bitter stimuli at intervals; he found real but minute variation, and his hypothesis generally holds up; 'The problem isn't with Hanig's findings. It's how he decided to present that information' — his line graph plots the relative change in sensitivity for each taste from one point to the next, NOT against other tastes; Edwin G. Boring, a Harvard psychology professor, reimagined that graph in the 1940s in Sensation and Perception in the History of Experimental Psychology, again with no meaningful scale, sectioning off each taste's most sensitive area into the familiar map; Hanig never tested umami; in 1965 the surgeon T. R. Bull found subjects whose chorda tympani had been cut in medical procedures reported no loss of taste; in 1993 Linda Bartoshuk found that anaesthetising the chorda tympani left subjects still perceiving sweet, and perceiving it more intensely; and modern receptor work finds each receptor type across all taste areas in the mouth, rather than sweet at the front and bitter at the back.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 18 Aug 2026. NO figure beat. Candidates considered and cut: 1901, 1942 and 1965 are dates, and 4 (the number of tastes on the map) is a count that happens to exist. The opening beat deliberately corrects the DEBUNKING rather than the myth: the widely repeated version of the correction is that Boring mistranslated Hanig's German, and Munger's account puts the failure somewhere more specific and more interesting — the measurements were sound, and what broke was an unscaled graph, first Hanig's own and then Boring's redrawing of it. Boring's date is given as the 1940s, not 1942, because the source says 'in the 1940s'; 1942 is the commonly cited publication year but was not read here. Deliberately not said: that Hanig was wrong — he was not, and the beats credit his measurements. Also not said: any claim that the tongue is uniformly sensitive, which overcorrects; the real finding is that the differences are minute and every receptor type appears everywhere there are taste buds. Virginia Collings's 1974 replication is real and often cited but appears in no source read here, so it gets no beat.

beats.lead: The tongue map was not a mistranslation
beats.text: It was a graph with no scale.
beats.note: That is the correction to the correction. The 1901 measurements were sound. What failed was the drawing: each taste's sensitivity plotted against itself, point to point along the tongue, and never against the other tastes.

beats.name: David Hanig
beats.role: He dripped salt, sweet, sour and bitter around the rim of the tongue — the taste belt, he called it — and measured how much of each it took before you noticed. He found real differences. They were minute.

beats.lead: Forty years later, at Harvard
beats.text: Edwin Boring redrew the curves.
beats.note: In Sensation and Perception in the History of Experimental Psychology, again with no meaningful scale. Each taste's most sensitive spot became a territory with a border. That is the diagram that reached the textbooks.

beats.lead: The nerve settles it
beats.text: Cut it, and the sweet stays.
beats.note: In 1965 the surgeon T. R. Bull found patients whose chorda tympani had been severed reported no loss of taste. In 1993 Linda Bartoshuk anaesthetised the same nerve and subjects tasted sweet more intensely, not less.

beats.text: Hanig never tested umami. Nobody had named it yet.

beats.line: Every receptor type turns up wherever there are taste buds.

sources: https://boingboing.net/2005/11/08/wifi-isnt-short-for.html — Cory Doctorow (Boing Boing, 8 Nov 2005) publishing the full statement of Phil Belanger, a founding member of the Wi-Fi Alliance who presided over the name selection: "Wi-Fi doesn't stand for anything. It is not an acronym. There is no meaning." Establishes that Interbrand created the name and the yin-yang logo; that the alliance (originally the Wireless Ethernet Compatibility Alliance) hired Interbrand because it needed something catchier than "IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence"; that Wi-Fi was chosen from a list of ten names Interbrand proposed; and that "The Standard for Wireless Fidelity" was a tag line invented AFTER the name by the six-member board, ran about a year (circa 2000), then was dropped — Belanger calls it a "mistake" that "diluted the brand."

https://www.mentalfloss.com/technology/what-does-wi-fi-stand-for — Mental Floss (7 May 2024), read directly. Quotes the Oxford English Dictionary: "Subsequent rationalization of this word as a shortening of wireless fidelity is spurious." Corroborates the Belanger account and the WECA/Interbrand/hi-fi-pun history, and gives the standardisation backdrop (FCC opened spectrum 1985; IEEE ratified 802.11 in 1997).

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi_Alliance — read for the dates used: "In 1999, pioneers ... formed the Wireless Ethernet Compatibility Alliance (WECA) and branded the new technology Wi-Fi" (cited to Littman, Building Broadband Networks, CRC Press 2002); and "WECA renamed itself the Wi-Fi Alliance in 2002" (cited to InternetNews, 2 Oct 2002).
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 20 Aug 2026. No figure beat: the available numbers are 10 (names Interbrand proposed) and 6 (board members who wrote the tag line); both are true and both are addresses, not facts, so neither earns 300px — the same discipline as the QWERTY entry. The OED line is quoted as read in Mental Floss, which cites the OED entry; I did not open the paywalled OED entry myself, so the beat says "the dictionary calls it spurious" rather than quoting a page I read. Deliberately not said: that Interbrand intended Wi to mean wireless — Mental Floss says it is only "generally believed" the pun drew on hi-fi, and Belanger's whole point is that the name is a coined brand with no literal decomposition, so the entry does not invent a hidden meaning to then debunk. The 1999 credit is the year WECA branded the technology Wi-Fi; some secondary sources say August 1999 specifically, not used here because no primary for the month was read.

beats.lead: The expansion in every router manual
beats.text: Wi-Fi is short for Wireless Fidelity.
beats.note: The dictionary calls that reading spurious. Phil Belanger, who ran the naming, is blunter: it is not an acronym, and there is no meaning.

beats.name: Interbrand
beats.role: The alliance behind the new 802.11b radio could not market "IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence," so it hired the agency that had named Prozac and Compaq. What came back was Wi-Fi — a pun on hi-fi, chosen from a list of ten.

beats.lead: Wireless Fidelity came afterwards
beats.text: The name was chosen first. The meaning was bolted on.
beats.note: Some board members could not stomach a name that explained nothing, so they added the tag line "The Standard for Wireless Fidelity." It ran about a year, then was quietly retired.

beats.lead: And it falls apart on contact
beats.text: The group never wrote a standard.
beats.note: It certifies that devices interoperate; the standard is IEEE's. So the phrase is wrong on both words — Belanger's own verdict is that it only diluted the brand.

beats.text: The man who picked the name spent years asking people to forget the tag line.

beats.line: You connect to a pun, not an acronym.

sources: https://www.bluetooth.com/about-us/bluetooth-origin/ — the Bluetooth SIG's official "Origin of the name" page, read directly. Establishes: the name "is not an acronym and doesn't stand for anything"; it is King Harald "Bluetooth" Gormsson, known for uniting Denmark and Norway in 958 and for a dead, dark blue/grey tooth that earned the nickname; that in 1996 Intel, Ericsson and Nokia met to standardise a short-range radio and Jim Kardach of Intel proposed "Bluetooth" as a temporary code name (quoted: "King Harald Bluetooth...was famous for uniting Scandinavia just as we intended to unite the PC and cellular industries with a short-range wireless link"); that the intended "serious" names were RadioWire or PAN, that PAN led but returned tens of thousands of search hits, that RadioWire's trademark search could not finish before launch, so the placeholder shipped and spread; and that the logo is a bind rune merging the Younger Futhark runes Hagall (ᚼ) and Bjarkan (ᛒ), Harald's initials.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 20 Aug 2026. Sourced entirely to the Bluetooth SIG's own origin page (primary). No figure beat: the only number is 958 (the year Harald united Denmark and Norway), and a date does not earn 300px — it belongs in the credit beat, where it sits. Deliberately not said: the book Kardach was reportedly reading (widely said to be a Viking historical novel); the SIG page does not name it and no primary naming it was read, so no beat claims it. Also not asserted as settled: WHY Harald was called Blatand — the SIG says a dead blue/grey tooth, but the epithet's origin is debated, so the beat reports the SIG's account rather than stating it as fact. The runes ᚼ and ᛒ are included as glyphs; if the render font lacks Younger Futhark they show as tofu, so the sentence also names them "his H and his B" and survives without the glyphs — worth a font check before publishing.

beats.lead: The icon in your status bar
beats.text: It is a dead king's initials.
beats.note: Not a waveform, not an acronym. Two Younger Futhark runes — ᚼ and ᛒ, his H and his B — pressed into one mark.

beats.name: Harald Gormsson
beats.role: King of Denmark, called Blatand — Bluetooth — for a dead, blue-grey tooth. He pulled the Danish tribes together and brought in Norway. That uniting is the entire reason the name was chosen.

beats.name: Jim Kardach, Intel
beats.role: In a meeting to make Intel, Ericsson and Nokia's radios talk to each other, he offered "Bluetooth" as a throwaway codename — a king who united Scandinavia, for a link meant to unite the PC and the phone.

beats.lead: It was never supposed to ship
beats.text: The real names were RadioWire and PAN.
beats.note: PAN led until a search returned tens of thousands of hits. RadioWire's trademark check could not clear in time for launch. So the placeholder went out, and spread before anyone could replace it.

beats.text: Marketing's "really cool" name never arrived. The codename ate it.

beats.line: You pair with a tenth-century king every day.

sources: https://medium.com/readme-mic/a-conversation-with-norm-cox-creator-of-the-hamburger-menu-c913daea5f9e — Tri Vo's 2015 interview with Norm Cox, read directly. In his own words: the "hamburger" widget was designed "out of pure necessity" for the Xerox Star, constrained by the display of the day (black and white, 72 dpi); the Star's window header could not fit all the command buttons, especially when resizing, and could not grow vertically, so he needed a button to hold the extra/related commands — "this resulted in the hamburger widget with the three lines that represented a drop-down menu"; and that he did not know it had "blew up," or was even called a "hamburger," until a journalist called to interview him about two years earlier (~2013), guessing a later UI designer re-drew three lines and "wasn't even aware of its prior existence on the Xerox Star."

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburger_button — read for dates and the Unicode detail. Norm Cox designed the icon for the Xerox Star, introduced 1981; Cox quote that it was rendered in about 16x16 pixels ("or possibly 13x13") and meant to "mimic the look of the resulting displayed menu list"; it appeared in Windows 1.0 (1985), vanished by Windows 2.0, and did not return to Windows until the Windows 10 Anniversary Update (2016); its mobile resurgence began around 2009; and it is not a text character in Unicode, so designers substitute look-alikes such as U+2261 ≡ (IDENTICAL TO) or U+2630 ☰ (TRIGRAM FOR HEAVEN).
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 20 Aug 2026. No figure beat: the tempting number is the icon's pixel size, but Cox himself hedges it ("16x16 ... or possibly 13x13"), so stamping a hard 16 at 300px would claim a precision the source disclaims — the pixel constraint is carried in a note instead. 1981 is the Xerox Star's introduction year (Wikipedia); Cox says "1980-ish" in the interview, so the entry ties the date to the machine's release rather than to the drawing. Deliberately not said: that today's mobile designers copied the Star — Cox's own guess is the opposite, that someone re-invented three lines without knowing the Star had them, so the entry frames it as re-discovery, not lineage. The glyphs ≡ and ☰ are included; ≡ (U+2261) is near-universal but ☰ (U+2630) may tofu, so the sentence names it "the I Ching's trigram for heaven" and survives without the glyph — font check before publishing.

beats.lead: The three lines you tap to open a menu
beats.text: They were drawn in 1981.
beats.note: Not for a phone — for the Xerox Star, a black-and-white office workstation. Norm Cox needed somewhere to park the buttons that would not fit across a window's title bar.

beats.name: Norm Cox
beats.role: He drew the Star's icons, including the dog-eared page still used for "document." The menu mark had to read at about sixteen pixels square: three bars, a shrunk picture of the list that would drop down.

beats.lead: Then it kept disappearing
beats.text: Windows had it in 1985, then threw it away.
beats.note: It shipped in Windows 1.0, vanished by Windows 2.0, and did not return to Windows until 2016. Phones revived it around 2009, when screens got small again.

beats.lead: It has no letter of its own
beats.text: There is no hamburger in Unicode.
beats.note: So designers fake it — usually with the maths sign for "identical to," ≡, or the I Ching's trigram for heaven, ☰. The icon a billion people tap is borrowed punctuation.

beats.text: Cox learned it was everywhere — and called a hamburger — from a reporter's phone call, thirty years on.

beats.line: The newest button on your phone turns forty-five this year.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin_Mann — read for dates: Mann founded 43 Folders in September 2004; he "coined and popularized the concept of Inbox Zero, writing a series of articles in 2006 on 43 Folders," originally proposing an "Inbox DMZ" (Fresh Start: The Email DMZ, 4 Jan 2006); and "In 2020 Mann stated he doesn't keep his inbox empty, and that the term has been misunderstood" (cited to Wired UK, 2 Jan 2020).

https://www.43folders.com/43-folders-series-inbox-zero — Merlin Mann's own site, read directly. The site describes itself as "about finding the time and attention to do your best creative work"; the Inbox Zero series frames the goal as processing messages "into appropriate actions as quickly as possible" and repeatedly warns "don't live in your Inbox"; and it records that the definitive Inbox Zero talk was "delivered on July 23, 2007 at a Google Tech Talk in Mountain View," a 58-minute video.

https://www.inc.com/betsy-mikel/the-guy-who-invented-inbox-zero-says-were-all-doing-it-wrong.html — Inc., 8 Jan 2020, read directly. Confirms Mann launched 43folders.com in 2004; that his own inbox "is full of clutter" and he says the popular practice is wrong; and that the app Mailbox built its entire product around hitting inbox zero (a gamified "You're all done" screen), which Dropbox acquired and shut down in 2016.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 20 Aug 2026. No figure beat: every candidate (2004, 2006, 2007, 2016) is a date, and "0" itself is the popular misreading, so enlarging it would restate the myth — the same reason the ten-thousand-hours entry refused to enlarge 10,000. Deliberately not quoted: the widely-circulated line that the zero means "the amount of time your brain is in your inbox." It is attributed to Mann all over the web, but I did not read it at a primary source, so the entry states the substance — the zero is about attention, not message count — which the sources I did read support (the site's own "time and attention" framing; his 2020 statement that the empty-inbox reading misses the point) without putting quotation marks around a line I did not verify.

beats.lead: The goal everyone chases
beats.text: Inbox Zero means an empty inbox.
beats.note: The man who named it does not keep his empty, and says that reading misses the whole point. The zero was never the message count.

beats.name: Merlin Mann
beats.role: On his site 43 Folders — "finding the time and attention to do your best creative work" — he coined Inbox Zero. The zero he meant was the attention you cede to email, not the number of messages in the box.

beats.lead: It was about not living in there
beats.text: Turn each message into an action, fast, then leave.
beats.note: That is the series' actual advice: convert mail to a next step as quickly as you can, and stop refreshing. Zero minutes with your brain stuck in the inbox — not zero emails.

beats.lead: Then an app hard-coded the wrong reading
beats.text: Mailbox gamified hitting zero.
beats.note: A cheerful "You're all done" over a changing photo, every time you emptied the box. Dropbox bought Mailbox and shut it down in 2016. The number won; the point was lost.

beats.text: In 2020 the inventor admitted his own inbox is full.

beats.line: Chase the attention, not the count.

sources: http://donhodges.com/how_high_can_you_get2.htm — Don Hodges, "Pac-Man's Split Screen Level Analyzed and Fixed" (2007), read directly, working from the disassembled arcade Z80 code. Establishes: Pac-Man stores the level in a single byte and counts the first board as level 0, so board 256 is internally 255 (#FF); the fruit-drawing routine loads the level and increments it with no carry-flag check, so at 256 the count wraps to 0 and the draw-loop counter rolls to 255 — running 256 times and stamping up to 512 bytes (#200) of memory from past the fruit table onto the right of the screen; that the game does NOT crash (Pac-Man and ghosts keep working, the left maze is intact); that a few of the garbled bytes happen to be edible-dot codes; that the board therefore cannot be cleared; and that Hodges fixed it by changing nine bytes of code (plus two checksum bytes) so board 256 draws seven keys and can be finished.

https://pacman.fandom.com/wiki/Map_256_Glitch — Pac-Man Wiki, read directly (cites Hodges). Establishes the on-screen dot arithmetic: clearing a board requires eating 244 Pac-Dots; the corrupted board holds 122 dots on the intact left half and 9 on the garbled right, 131 in all — far short of 244, so the level is unwinnable; and that the theoretical maximum score on the original is 3,333,360.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 20 Aug 2026. Figure beat is 131 (dots), not 256: 256 is the headline everyone already knows and enlarging it just restates the topic; 131 is the finding that makes "unwinnable" concrete — the board simply does not contain the 244 dots the game demands. Numbers deliberately NOT enlarged: 256 (the topic), 255 (the true byte ceiling, but an awkward unit) and 3,333,360 (the max score — real but trivia, and a seven-digit value would swamp the card). Honesty on 131: the Pac-Man Wiki notes the 9 right-side dots regenerate after a lost life, so a player can eat at most ~176 across deaths — still short of 244; the figure's context says the board "holds" 131 dots (true of a single pass) and that 244 can never be reached (true regardless), and this nuance is recorded here rather than on screen. Not claimed: any first-perfect-game record (the well-known 3,333,360 claim is entangled in a disputed-score controversy), so no player is named. Not called a "crash," because the disassembly shows the game keeps running — only the fruit routine misdraws.

beats.lead: Pac-Man has no final level
beats.text: The ending is a byte running out of room.
beats.note: No one designed a board 256. The game keeps the level in a single byte, which cannot count past 255 — and 256 is what spills out when it tries.

beats.context: Every dot the broken board contains — 122 on the intact left, 9 in the garbled right. Clearing a board takes 244. The count can never be reached, so the level cannot end.

beats.name: Don Hodges
beats.role: He disassembled the arcade code and found it: at board 256 the level counter wraps to zero, and the routine that paints the fruit is told to draw 256 of them — smearing 512 bytes of unrelated program across the right of the screen.

beats.lead: It is not a crash
beats.text: The game runs fine. It draws the wrong memory.
beats.note: Pac-Man still moves, the ghosts still hunt, the left maze is perfect. A few of the garbled bytes even happen to be edible dots. Only the fruit routine has lost the plot.

beats.text: Hodges fixed it in nine bytes. The famous wall was one missing check the whole time.

beats.line: Pac-Man ends where a byte does.

sources: https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/donkey-kong-mistranslation/ (Snopes, David Mikkelson, published 24 February 2001; read in full 27 August 2026): established that the popular legend that 'Donkey Kong' was a mistranslated, mistyped or misheard 'Monkey Kong' has no supporting evidence; that Shigeru Miyamoto, who built the 1981 game after being asked to salvage the failed arcade title 'Radarscope', has repeatedly said he used 'donkey' to convey stubbornness and 'Kong' to invoke a gorilla; that Miyamoto stated at the later Universal trial that 'King Kong' was treated in Japan as a generic term for a large, scary ape; and that Donkey Kong earned Nintendo of America about 100 million dollars in its first year.

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/746/112/30961/ (US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, Universal City Studios, Inc. v. Nintendo Co., 746 F.2d 112, decided 4 October 1984; read in full 27 August 2026): established that Universal sued Nintendo in 1982 claiming Donkey Kong infringed and diluted its King Kong trademark; that Nintendo's counsel was John J. Kirby, Jr.; that the district court under Judge Sweet granted Nintendo summary judgment and the appeals court affirmed on the ground that there was no likelihood of consumer confusion, calling Donkey Kong 'at best... a parody of King Kong'; and, in footnote 1, that in a 1975 California case Universal had itself sought a declaration that it could remake King Kong because the story was in the public domain.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 27 August 2026 against Snopes and the Second Circuit opinion, both read in full. The correction is twofold: the 'Monkey Kong mistranslation' is an unevidenced legend, and Nintendo's win did not turn on the public-domain point that the popular retelling stresses. The appeals court affirmed only on no likelihood of confusion and expressly declined to decide the public-domain and estoppel questions in footnote 3, so the entry states that Universal had argued King Kong was public domain in 1975 as fact and as part of Nintendo's defence, without claiming it was the stated ground of the ruling. No figure beat: the money figures, about 100 million dollars in the first year and over 180 million dollars from roughly 60,000 machines by the time of the suit, are real but incidental to a story about a name and a lawsuit, so none is enlarged. Deliberately not said: the widely repeated claim that Nintendo's Kirby character was named after lawyer John Kirby, which Nintendo has never confirmed; and the fax and phone-line versions of the legend, whose mutual inconsistency is itself the tell.

beats.lead: The name is supposed to be a mistake
beats.text: 'Monkey Kong', garbled into 'Donkey'.
beats.note: The legend says a blurred fax, or a bad phone line, turned 'Monkey' into 'Donkey' before anyone caught it. It is retold everywhere. There is no evidence for any version of it.

beats.name: Shigeru Miyamoto
beats.role: Asked to rescue a failed arcade game, he built Donkey Kong instead. He has said he chose 'donkey' from a dictionary to mean stubborn, and 'Kong' for a gorilla. At trial he added that in Japan 'King Kong' just meant any big, scary ape.

beats.lead: 1982, Universal City Studios sues
beats.text: Nintendo has stolen King Kong, they say.
beats.note: Universal claimed Donkey Kong infringed its King Kong trademark. Awkwardly, seven years earlier Universal had gone to court to argue the opposite: that the King Kong story belonged to no one, and was in the public domain.

beats.lead: Nintendo won
beats.text: The two apes were not alike enough to confuse anyone.
beats.note: The court ruled for Nintendo in 1984 on a plain ground: no one would mistake a barrel-throwing cartoon for King Kong. Donkey Kong was, it wrote, 'at best... a parody'. Nintendo's lawyer was John Kirby.

beats.text: The studio that owned King Kong had already told a court that King Kong belonged to everyone. It lost to the cartoon ape anyway.

beats.line: A dictionary, a gorilla, and a lawsuit the giant lost.

sources: https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/09/professors-perceptron-paved-way-ai-60-years-too-soon (Cornell Chronicle, Melanie Lefkowitz, 25 September 2019; read in full 27 August 2026): established that in July 1958 the US Office of Naval Research demonstrated Frank Rosenblatt's Perceptron on a five-ton, room-sized IBM 704, which after 50 trials taught itself to tell cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right; that Rosenblatt, a research psychologist at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, called it 'the first machine which is capable of having an original idea'; that the New York Times headline read 'NEW NAVY DEVICE LEARNS BY DOING: Psychologist Shows Embryo of Computer Designed to Read and Grow Wiser' and the New Yorker called it 'the first serious rival to the human brain ever devised'; that the perceptron had a single layer while modern networks have millions; that its rise and fall helped usher in the 'AI winter'; that Rosenblatt drowned in 1971 on his 43rd birthday; and that his Mark I perceptron now sits in the Smithsonian.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceptrons_(book) (Wikipedia, 'Perceptrons (book)'; read in full 27 August 2026): established that Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published Perceptrons in 1969; that its proofs showed a single-layer perceptron cannot compute certain simple predicates including the XOR function; that the book is commonly credited with helping shift AI funding toward symbolic systems and contributing to the AI winter; and, as a complicating point, that this causal story is contested, with Minsky and Papert themselves later saying research waned for other reasons and critics such as Bernard Widrow calling the proofs largely irrelevant.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 27 August 2026 against the Cornell Chronicle and the Wikipedia article on the Minsky and Papert book, both read in full. The reel's point is that the AI hype cycle is old: in 1958 the press said the brain had a rival, and eleven years later a single-layer perceptron was shown unable to compute XOR. No figure beat: the supporting numbers, five tons, IBM 704, 50 trials, 1958, 1969 and age 43, are scene-setting rather than the claim, so none is enlarged. Deliberately not said: the much-quoted line that the 1958 New York Times report predicted a machine that would 'walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence', because the original NYT article was not read in full here; only the headline and the New Yorker line, both quoted verbatim by Cornell, are used. The claim that the Minsky and Papert book 'killed' neural networks is softened to 'helped usher in' the AI winter, because that causation is disputed in the sources. This is a distinct episode from the existing ai-winter-1973 topic, which concerns the later Lighthill report in Britain.

beats.lead: 1958. The US Navy shows off a machine that learns.
beats.text: The press says the human brain finally has a rival.
beats.note: The New Yorker called the Perceptron 'the first serious rival to the human brain ever devised'. The New York Times ran the headline 'New Navy Device Learns By Doing'.

beats.name: Frank Rosenblatt
beats.role: A Cornell psychologist. His Perceptron ran on a five-ton IBM 704, and after 50 trials it taught itself to tell a card marked on the left from one marked on the right. He called it 'the first machine capable of having an original idea'.

beats.lead: Then the maths caught up
beats.text: It could not tell whether two inputs disagreed.
beats.note: In 1969 Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert proved a single-layer perceptron cannot compute XOR, one of the simplest logic functions there is. Rosenblatt's machine had one layer. Today's networks have millions.

beats.lead: The money went cold
beats.text: An AI winter set in.
beats.note: Funding for neural networks dried up, and the field turned elsewhere for years. Rosenblatt did not see the thaw: he drowned in 1971, sailing, on his forty-third birthday.

beats.text: The machine that would rival the brain had been on the right track all along, about sixty years too soon.

beats.line: His Mark I perceptron now sits in the Smithsonian.

sources: https://www.w3.org/Protocols/HTTP/HTRESP.html (W3C, 'Status codes in HTTP', a historic CERN and W3C document dated 1992; read in full 27 August 2026): established that HTTP groups its status codes by leading digit, that the '4xx codes are intended for cases in which the client seems to have erred' while 5xx codes are for server errors, and that 404 is defined as 'Not found: The server has not found anything matching the URI given', listed alongside 400 Bad request, 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden.

https://queenofsubtle.com/404/?page_id=1921 (404 Research Lab, 'a brief history of 404'; read in full 27 August 2026): established that the HTTP status codes were defined by Tim Berners-Lee as part of the early HTTP specification and were modelled on the older FTP reply codes; that in 404 the leading 4 marks a client error; and, quoting a visitor to CERN, that there is no room 404 at CERN, the offices on that floor starting at 410, so the 'named after a room' story is a myth.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 27 August 2026 against the W3C historic status-code document, read in full, and the 404 Research Lab history, read in full. The load-bearing correction rests on the primary W3C page: 404 is simply the 'Not found' entry in HTTP's numbered scheme, 4xx meaning the client erred. No figure beat: 404 is a code, an address in a list, not a quantity, so it is never enlarged, the same discipline the moth topic used for its relay number. The 'no room 404 at CERN' detail and the FTP lineage come from the 404 Research Lab, the former from an anecdotal visitor account rather than an official CERN statement, so the reel treats the systematic scheme as the answer and the absent room as corroboration. Deliberately not said as fact: the specific 'offices start at 410' room number; the beats claim only that no room 404 existed. The variant legends, that it was Berners-Lee's office or the first server's room, are named as the myth, not endorsed.

beats.lead: You hit a dead link. 404. Not found.
beats.text: The story says it is named after a room at CERN.
beats.note: The legend: room 404 held the web's first server, or Tim Berners-Lee's office, and anything the server could not locate was 'not found in room 404'. It is told constantly. It is also wrong.

beats.lead: 404 is not a place. It is a position in a list.
beats.text: The 4 means you erred. The rest just means 'not found'.
beats.note: In HTTP every reply carries a status code. Codes starting with 4 mean the client made the mistake, a bad or missing request. 404 sits with 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden. Nothing more.

beats.name: Tim Berners-Lee
beats.role: Wrote the codes into the young web's specification at CERN. The definition has read the same ever since: 'The server has not found anything matching the URI given.' A slot in a table, not a door.

beats.text: There was never a room 404 at CERN. There is only the list, and the fourth kind of error on it.

beats.line: The web's most famous dead end is a filing decision, not a place.

sources: https://graphics.stanford.edu/~dk/google_name_origin.html (Stanford University, David Koller, January 2004; read in full 27 August 2026): established, from Koller's Stanford colleagues in the office where Google was born, that in 1996 Larry Page and Sergey Brin called their search engine 'BackRub'; that in September 1997, brainstorming a new name, Sean Anderson suggested 'googolplex' and Page shortened it to 'googol'; that Anderson, checking whether the domain was free, mistakenly searched for 'google.com', which was available; and that Page registered google.com that day, the registration record dating from 15 September 1997.

https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/SH/kasner_sh.pdf (MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, 'Edward Kasner and how Google got its Name'; read in full 27 August 2026): established, quoting Kasner and Newman's 1940 book Mathematics and the Imagination, that 'googol' was coined in 1920 by Kasner's nine-year-old nephew Milton Sirotta as a name for 1 followed by a hundred zeros, and that a googolplex is a still larger number, 1 followed by zeros 'until you get tired'.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 27 August 2026 against David Koller's Stanford account, read in full, and the St Andrews MacTutor page, read in full. The correction is that Google is not a tidy homage to the number googol but a misspelling of it, kept only because the misspelt domain happened to be free. Figure beat: '100 zeros' is enlarged because the hundredness is the definition of googol and the reason the founders reached for the word; it is a whole number with a short unit, and it is the fact, not an address, unlike Page's office room number 360, which is left out. The naming account is Sean Anderson's recollection as recorded by Koller around 2004, several years after 1997, and is presented as such rather than as a contemporaneous record. Deliberately not said: the popular line that a googol exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe, broadly true but whose specific figure was not read in a source here; and any claim that Sergey Brin was in the room, since Koller places only Anderson and Page at the whiteboard.

beats.lead: Google is named after googol, the number.
beats.text: Except nobody meant to spell it that way.
beats.note: The founders were reaching for 'googol', a mathematician's word for an enormous number. The company carries a typo of it, kept because the misspelling was the domain that happened to be free.

beats.context: A googol is 1 followed by a hundred zeros. A nine-year-old, Milton Sirotta, coined the word in 1920; his uncle, the mathematician Edward Kasner, wrote it into a book. Google's founders were aiming for it.

beats.name: Sean Anderson
beats.role: A Stanford graduate student sharing Larry Page's office. Brainstorming names, he went to check whether 'googol' was a free domain, but typed 'google.com' by mistake. It was available. Page registered it the same day, 15 September 1997.

beats.text: The number was named by a child. The company was named by a typo. Neither was the plan.

beats.line: A misspelt search for a schoolboy's number, registered in an afternoon.

sources: https://www.toureiffel.paris/en/the-monument/eiffel-tower-and-science (Official Eiffel Tower website, Societe d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel, 'The Eiffel Tower and science'; read in full 27 August 2026): established that the tower was to be destroyed 20 years after construction; that Gustave Eiffel promoted scientific uses to save it; that on 5 November 1898 Eugene Ducretet made the first wireless telegraphy contact between the tower and the Pantheon; that from 1903 Eiffel funded Captain Gustave Ferrie's military wireless experiments from the tower, whose concession was due to end in 1909; that in 1909 an underground military radiotelegraphy station was set up and the City of Paris renewed the concession on 1 January 1910; and that in the First World War the tower's station intercepted German communications before the Battle of the Marne.

https://www.toureiffel.paris/en/the-monument/history (Official Eiffel Tower website, 'Origins and Construction of the Eiffel Tower'; read in full 27 August 2026): established that the tower was built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle marking the centenary of the French Revolution, stood 300 metres tall, and was completed on 31 March 1889; and that in 1887 a 'Protest against the Tower of Monsieur Eiffel', signed by figures including Guy de Maupassant, Charles Gounod, Alexandre Dumas junior and Charles Garnier, condemned the 'useless and monstrous' tower as a 'hateful column of bolted sheet metal'.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 27 August 2026 against two pages of the official Eiffel Tower website, both read in full. The correction is that the tower everyone treats as the permanent symbol of Paris was a temporary exhibit, licensed for 20 years and due for demolition in 1909, and that it was saved not by affection but by its usefulness as a radio aerial. Figure beat: '20 years' is enlarged because the length of the concession is the crux the whole story turns on, a whole number with a short unit; the height, 300 metres, and the wartime ranges, up to 6,000 km, are left in prose because they are scenery to this particular story, not its point. Deliberately not foregrounded: the official site's line that the tower's station helped expose the spy Mata Hari, which is popular but historically embellished, so it is omitted rather than leaned on; and the tower's later growth to 324 metres with television aerials, which belongs to a different chapter.

beats.lead: The symbol of Paris was built to be scrapped.
beats.text: The Eiffel Tower was only ever meant to be temporary.
beats.note: Raised for the 1889 World's Fair, 300 metres of iron marking a century since the Revolution, it was an exhibit, not a monument. The city fully intended to take it down again.

beats.context: That was the length of Gustave Eiffel's permit. When it ran out, the tower was to be dismantled and sold for scrap. The date set for its demolition was 1909.

beats.lead: Paris did not even like it
beats.text: Its own artists signed a protest to stop it.
beats.note: In 1887 Maupassant, Dumas, Gounod and others petitioned against the 'useless and monstrous' tower, a 'hateful column of bolted sheet metal' over the city. The most famous shape in Paris began as an eyesore.

beats.name: Gustave Eiffel
beats.role: To save his tower, he made it useful. He funded army wireless experiments from the top, and by 1909 a military radio station beneath it made it indispensable. Paris renewed the lease, and the demolition never came.
