beats.lead: Berlin, early 1900s.
beats.text: A horse could allegedly do arithmetic.
beats.note: Hans tapped out answers to maths, calendar and spelling questions with his hoof. A formal commission of thirteen experts examined him in 1904 and found no trick at all.

beats.lead: Then a psychologist checked again.
beats.text: In 1907, Oskar Pfungst found the trick anyway.
beats.note: Hans wasn't calculating. He was reading his questioner's posture and expression, and stopping the instant they subtly relaxed.

beats.context: Correct, when Hans could see a questioner who already knew the answer. Hide that questioner from view and he collapsed to 6 percent.

beats.name: Oskar Pfungst
beats.role: The psychologist assigned to re-test Hans. He proved his theory by becoming the horse himself: tapping out numbers by hand, he produced the same involuntary tell in the people standing beside him.

beats.text: The pattern outlived the horse.
beats.note: "Clever Hans effect" is now the term for an AI model that looks intelligent while actually keying off a spurious signal, an image classifier reading text in a photo instead of the picture itself.

beats.line: The trick a horse pulled in 1904 is still fooling machines.

beats.lead: You know the year Columbus crossed the Atlantic.

beats.note: Not legend, a dated find: European wood, cut with metal tools nobody in the area had, at the northern tip of Newfoundland.

beats.lead: The site was found in 1960.

beats.note: Archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad excavated it through the 1960s and dated it to "around 1000 AD" by comparing it with sites in Greenland and Iceland, a good estimate, not a year.

beats.lead: In 2021, a solar storm did what shovels couldn't.
beats.text: A cosmic-ray spike from the year 993 is baked into tree rings everywhere on Earth.
beats.note: Researchers counted growth rings outward from that marked ring, on wood the Norse had felled and shaped, straight to the year they cut it.

beats.context: The exact year, from 127 radiocarbon measurements across four wooden objects. Not "around 1000". Not a century. One year.

beats.name: Margot Kuitems
beats.role: Led the University of Groningen team that published the date in Nature, using the 993 solar storm as a fixed marker buried in the rings of every sample tested.

sources: http://doc.cat-v.org/economics/parkinsons-law/: the original essay text, read in full. Establishes: byline credits "Northcote Parkinson, Raffles Professor of History at the University of Singapore"; first appeared in The Economist in November 1955; opens with the (explicitly illustrative) story of an elderly lady spending a whole day mailing a postcard, an hour finding it, another finding her spectacles, half an hour finding the address, an hour and a quarter composing it, twenty minutes deciding about an umbrella, against a busy person's three minutes; states "Factor I: An official wants to multiply subordinates, not rivals" and "Factor II: Officials make work for each other."

https://www.usni.org/magazines/naval-history-magazine/1994/december-1/challenging-parkinsons-law: Jon Sumida (associate professor of history, University of Maryland), "Challenging Parkinson's Law," Naval History Magazine, December 1994, read in full. Establishes Parkinson's actual career (PhD in history, King's College London; Master of the Royal Naval College Dartmouth; Lecturer in History, Liverpool; Raffles Professor of History at the University of Malaya; died 9 March 1993 aged 83; wrote over 60 books, mostly serious naval history); that the postcard story was "obviously fictitious" by Parkinson's own framing; that the collected book sold nearly a quarter of a million copies in two years; Parkinson's published Admiralty table (1914: 2,000 officials to 1928: 3,569, a 78.45% rise, against a 67.74% fall in capital ships and a 31.5% fall in personnel); that Parkinson never disclosed the source of these statistics; that an independent check against the actual Navy Lists found the true 1914 figure was about a quarter lower than Parkinson's, which raises the honest percentage increase to roughly 120%; and that this growth tracks almost exactly with World War One's demands, wartime equipment failures, a hiring surge to match the Ministry of Munitions' paperwork, and the mass hiring of lower-paid women clerical staff, none of which Parkinson's essay mentions.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 30 Aug 2026 against both sources read in full. Deliberately not framed as "Parkinson lied": Sumida's actual point is subtler, the true growth was bigger than Parkinson claimed, but it lines up with an omitted war, not a universal law. Also not claimed: Sumida's aside that Walt Disney reportedly considered a film adaptation, since Sumida himself hedges that detail as "reputedly". One date conflict handled here: Sumida's article states the Economist piece appeared in 1958, but the essay's own byline and multiple independent sources date it to November 1955 (1958 is when the collected book followed); 1955 is used, since it is the date on the primary text itself.

beats.lead: The essay opens with a woman spending all day mailing a postcard.
beats.text: Parkinson admitted upfront that story was made up.
beats.note: The real piece was a satirical nine-page article for The Economist in November 1955, and it's still quoted today as if it were a study.

beats.lead: His actual evidence was British Admiralty staffing, 1914 to 1928.
beats.text: Officials up 78 percent, while the fleet shrank by two-thirds.
beats.note: It reads like scientific proof. Parkinson never disclosed where the numbers came from.

beats.lead: In 1994, a naval historian checked the real Navy Lists.
beats.text: The true growth was even bigger than Parkinson said, and so was the reason he left out.
beats.note: The honest 1914 baseline was lower, pushing the real increase closer to 120 percent. That surge tracks almost exactly with the paperwork of the First World War, which Parkinson's essay never mentions once.

beats.name: C. Northcote Parkinson
beats.role: A serious naval historian, Raffles Professor of History at the University of Malaya, in Singapore, whose nine-page joke in The Economist was collected into a book that sold nearly a quarter of a million copies in two years.

beats.context: Historian Jon Sumida's corrected 1914-to-1928 growth rate, using the actual Navy Lists rather than Parkinson's undisclosed source.

beats.line: A historian's joke about a war, mistaken for a law about offices.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpemba_effect: read in full. Establishes: Erasto Mpemba, a Tanzanian student, noticed in 1963 in Form 3 at Magamba Secondary School (Tanganyika) that a hot ice-cream mixture froze before a cold one in cookery class, and his teacher dismissed it; he later raised it with visiting physicist Denis Osborne at Mkwawa Secondary School; Osborne tested it with water at his own workplace and confirmed it; they co-published "Cool?" in Physics Education 4(3):172-175 in 1969, while Mpemba was studying at the College of African Wildlife Management; Aristotle wrote centuries earlier, "Hence many people, when they want to cool water quickly, begin by putting it in the sun"; Francis Bacon separately noted "slightly tepid water freezes more easily than that which is utterly cold"; Rene Descartes described the same pattern in his Discourse on the Method; in 2016, Henry Burridge and Paul Linden tested the time water takes to reach 0°C under tightly controlled conditions and concluded, in their own words, "We conclude, somewhat sadly, that there is no evidence to support meaningful observations of the Mpemba effect"; the article states physicists remain divided on the effect's reproducibility, precise definition and underlying mechanism.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5121640: Burridge, H.C. & Linden, P.F., "Questioning the Mpemba effect: hot water does not cool more quickly than cold," Scientific Reports 6:37665 (2016), cited via the Wikipedia article's direct quotation of the paper's conclusion; title, authors, journal and year corroborated independently.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 30 Aug 2026 against the Wikipedia article read in full, itself quoting both the 1969 and 2016 papers directly. Beats deliberately do not declare the effect either real or fake; the source is explicit that physicists remain split, and some later work on supercooling behaviour offers a narrower mechanism that could explain occasional genuine observations. No figure beat: the only numbers available are years and a temperature threshold (0°C), none of which is a count worth enlarging to 300px. Not claimed: any specific modern theoretical explanation for why the effect might sometimes appear, since the sources treat that as unsettled.

beats.lead: Tanganyika, 1963.
beats.text: A schoolboy watched his hot ice-cream mix freeze before the cold batch.
beats.note: Erasto Mpemba was in Form 3 at Magamba Secondary School. His teacher told him that was simply not possible.

beats.lead: Aristotle had already written the same thing, over two thousand years earlier.
beats.text: "Hence many people, when they want to cool water quickly, begin by putting it in the sun."
beats.note: Francis Bacon and Rene Descartes both noted it too, centuries before Mpemba was born. None of that stopped it from being named after him.

beats.name: Denis Osborne
beats.role: A physicist who met Mpemba at his next school, tested the claim with water back in his own lab, and confirmed it. They published together in Physics Education under the title "Cool?", while Mpemba was training at the College of African Wildlife Management, not a physics department.

beats.lead: The dramatic original numbers were never reliably repeated.
beats.text: In 2016, two researchers finally tested it under tightly controlled conditions.
beats.note: Henry Burridge and Paul Linden's own conclusion: "We conclude, somewhat sadly, that there is no evidence to support meaningful observations of the Mpemba effect."

beats.text: It's still taught as settled science in classrooms that have never settled it.

beats.line: Older than Aristotle. Still not proven.

sources: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/the-science-behind-honeys-eternal-shelf-life-1218690/ - Smithsonian Magazine (Natasha Geiling, 22 August 2013), read in full, quoting Amina Harris, executive director of the Honey and Pollination Center at the Robert Mondavi Institute, UC Davis, throughout. beats.lead: Archaeologists keep finding it
beats.text: Pots of honey, still good, sealed in tombs thousands of years old.
beats.note: Ancient Egyptian tombs in particular have turned up jars of honey that are millennia old and, once opened, still edible.

beats.lead: Bees dry it out first
beats.text: Raw nectar is mostly water. Finished honey barely is.
beats.note: Bees fan the nectar with their wings until most of the moisture is gone, leaving too little water for bacteria to get a foothold.

beats.lead: And it isn't just dry

beats.line: The only food built to outlive the jar it's in.

sources: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutnames_history.shtml - National Hurricane Center (NOAA), official naming-history page, read in full. beats.note: From 1953, when the US dropped a phonetic-alphabet naming scheme for storms, until 1979, hurricanes and tropical storms got female names only. No exceptions.

sources: https://www.history.com/articles/napoleon-complex-short - HISTORY (Una McIlvenna, 13 November 2019, updated 10 July 2025), read in full. Established that three French sources, Napoleon's valet Constant, General Gourgaud and his physician Francesco Antommarchi, recorded his height as '5 pieds 2 pouces'; that the French pouce measured 2.7cm against the imperial inch's 2.54cm, so the true figure converts to roughly 1.67 metres, just under 5'6", a little above the average French man of the early 1800s; that the 'short Napoleon' image is largely the work of British cartoonist James Gillray (1756-1815); that Gillray's earliest Napoleon cartoons (1798) showed him boastful but not small; that the diminutive 'Little Boney' image began with Gillray's 1803 cartoon 'Maniac-Ravings, or Little Boney in a Strong Fit', satirising a real outburst by Napoleon against the British ambassador, Lord Whitworth, at the Tuileries on 14 March 1803; that Gillray's 1805 cartoon 'The Plumb-pudding in Danger', described as probably the most famous political cartoon of all time, shows Napoleon at half the size of British Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger; and that Napoleon reportedly said Gillray 'did more than all the armies of Europe to bring me down'.

https://publicdomainreview.org/essay/little-boney/ - The Public Domain Review (Peter W. Walker, Assistant Professor of History, University of Wyoming, 21 March 2024), read in full. Established that Gillray produced around forty of the more than two thousand British satirical prints of Napoleon and that his were the most influential; that Gillray's 1798 cartoon still drew Napoleon as 'average-sized'; that the caricature shrank progressively through 1803 as invasion fears grew, becoming an animal in 'Death of the Corsican Fox', a baby in 'The Genius of France', and a six-inch Lilliputian dwarfed by an English giant in 'The King of Brobdingnag and Gulliver' (1804); that other cartoonists copied the trope; and that the term 'Napoleon Complex' derives directly from this caricature legacy and is described as being of questionable scientific validity.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 1 September 2026 against two sources read in full: HISTORY (Una McIlvenna) and The Public Domain Review (Peter W. Walker). Both agree on the core facts: three witnesses recorded 5 pieds 2 pouces, and the French pouce (2.7cm) versus English inch (2.54cm) explains the conversion to roughly 5'6". Deliberately not dated: exactly when Antommarchi recorded the measurement, since neither source states this, only that he was one of three witnesses; the credit beat instead uses Gillray's 1803 cartoon, which both sources date precisely. Not used: the sexual and Corsican-origin dimensions of Gillray's satire documented by the Public Domain Review, since they explain why the caricature worked rather than adding facts about Napoleon's actual height, and a short reel has no room to handle them responsibly. The 'Napoleon Complex' is explicitly not claimed as real psychology; the Public Domain Review calls its validity questionable, so the entry treats it only as the name the caricature left behind. No figure beat: the height converts to an approximation, 'roughly' and 'just under', not a single precise whole number that earns 300px. No em dashes, UK English, per run instruction.

beats.lead: Everyone knows Napoleon was short
beats.text: The men who measured him used a different ruler than you're picturing.
beats.note: His valet, a general and his own physician all recorded the same figure: five pieds, two pouces. That is French feet and inches, not English ones.

beats.lead: Convert it properly
beats.text: He comes out at roughly five foot six.
beats.note: A French pouce measured 2.7 centimetres against the English inch's 2.54. Do the sum and Napoleon lands just under 5'6", a little above the average French man of his time.

beats.name: James Gillray
beats.role: British cartoonist who invented 'Little Boney', a diminutive, raving caricature of Napoleon, in response to a real outburst the emperor made at the British ambassador on 14 March 1803. Gillray kept shrinking him for years afterwards.

beats.lead: The image only got smaller
beats.text: By 1804 he was drawn six inches tall.
beats.note: Gillray's cartoons showed Napoleon as an animal, then a baby, then a Lilliputian dwarfed by an English giant in 'The King of Brobdingnag and Gulliver'. The caricature, not the ruler, is what stuck.

beats.text: Napoleon himself said Gillray 'did more than all the armies of Europe to bring me down'.

beats.line: The cartoon won. The measurement lost.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAPTCHA - Wikipedia, read in full. Established that the term 'CAPTCHA' was coined in 2003 by Luis von Ahn, Manuel Blum, Nicholas J. Hopper and John Langford as a contrived acronym for 'Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart'; that a historically common type of CAPTCHA, the distorted-letter image, was 'first invented in 1997 by two groups working in parallel', before the name existed; that idrive.com began protecting its signup page with such a test in 2000 and prepared to file a patent (the Gausebeck-Levchin test); that PayPal used a similar test from 2001 as part of a fraud-prevention strategy, commercialised with help from co-founder Max Levchin; that reCAPTCHA was acquired by Google in 2009 and was then used, alongside CAPTCHA technology generally, to help digitise the archives of The New York Times and Google Books in 2011; and that a 2018 ACM CCS conference paper (Ye et al.) presented a deep-learning attack able to consistently solve all 11 text-CAPTCHA schemes used by the top 50 websites that year, trainable on as few as 500 real CAPTCHAs.

https://www.cs.cmu.edu/news/2009/google-inc-acquires-carnegie-mellon-spin-recaptcha-inc - Carnegie Mellon University's own news release (Byron Spice, 16 September 2009), read in full. Established that reCAPTCHA began as a research project of Luis von Ahn, assistant professor of computer science at Carnegie Mellon; that reCAPTCHAs, distorted words drawn from real printed text that optical-character-recognition software could not read, were introduced in 2007; that the company ReCAPTCHA Inc. was founded by von Ahn in 2008 and its acquisition by Google was announced on 16 September 2009; and that von Ahn remained on the CMU faculty while also working at Google's Pittsburgh office.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 1 September 2026 against Wikipedia's CAPTCHA article and Carnegie Mellon's own 2009 news release, both read in full. Deliberate correction: the common shorthand 'Luis von Ahn invented CAPTCHA' overstates his role. He and three co-authors coined the term and formalised the theory in a 2003 academic paper, but Wikipedia states a comparable test was 'first invented in 1997 by two groups working in parallel', with idrive.com (2000) and PayPal (2001) both using similar tests before the name existed. Von Ahn's clear, undisputed invention is reCAPTCHA in 2007, which is what the credit beat names instead. Not used: the popular claim that image-based reCAPTCHA challenges (traffic lights, crosswalks) train self-driving car AI; this appears often in general writing about reCAPTCHA but neither source read here states it, so it is left out rather than assumed. The '500 real CAPTCHAs' figure is Wikipedia's own citation of the 2018 Ye et al. paper, not independently read. No figure beat: 500 stays inside the kicker's sentence rather than being enlarged to 300px, since it belongs to a single claim about one study, not a standalone number the reel is built around. No em dashes, UK English, per run instruction.

beats.lead: The name is newer than the trick
beats.text: "CAPTCHA" was coined in 2003. The test already existed.
beats.note: Distorted-letter tests to block bots were already live in 2000, when idrive.com started using one, and PayPal adopted the same idea in 2001, years before anyone called it a CAPTCHA.

beats.lead: The name itself is a stretch
beats.text: It stands for something nobody would say out loud.
beats.note: Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. Von Ahn, Blum, Hopper and Langford built the acronym to fit the word, not the other way round.

beats.name: Luis von Ahn
beats.role: Carnegie Mellon researcher who turned the same idea into reCAPTCHA: instead of random letters, it showed real words that book-scanning software could not read, so solving the puzzle also helped digitise old text.

beats.lead: It worked well enough to sell
beats.text: Google bought it in 2009.
beats.note: The Carnegie Mellon spin-off was acquired within a year of being founded, and reCAPTCHA went on to help digitise The New York Times' archive and Google Books.

beats.text: A test built to prove you're not a computer. A 2018 study trained one to pass it using 500 examples.

beats.line: The gate built to keep machines out taught them to get through.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_scrolling - read in full 1 Sep 2026: infinite scroll was filed as a patent application on 14 February 2006 by Microsoft's Windows Live (MSN) Search image team; the feature shipped in the team's image search on 8 March 2006, the first product to ship with it; Microsoft engineering lead Hugh Williams has stated that he, Julie Farago and Nick Craswell were the inventors; Aza Raskin separately claimed credit for inventing infinite scroll in 2019.

https://hughewilliams.com/2012/03/06/ideas-and-invention-and-the-story-of-bings-image-search/ - read in full 1 Sep 2026, first-person account by named co-inventor Hugh Williams: he, Nick Craswell and Julie Farago built the feature into MSN Search's image results in 2005 after session data showed that while about 75% of web-search queries stayed on page one, only about 43% of image-search queries did, with some users paging into the twenties before clicking a result (his own example: a user who clicked a photo of a chocolate cake on roughly page twenty-something); the internal build was capped at 1,000 images, so it was never actually infinite.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aza_Raskin - read in full 1 Sep 2026: confirms Raskin's career timeline (born 1984; founded Humanized in 2005 after his father Jef Raskin's death); the article documents Raskin's other credited work, such as the tabnabbing phishing technique, but does not itself credit him with infinite scroll, consistent with the Infinite Scrolling article crediting Microsoft's team instead.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 1 Sep 2026 against three sources read in full. The Infinite Scrolling Wikipedia article carries an uncited claim that 'there is no evidence' for Raskin's 2019 claim; that line is not repeated here since it is itself flagged citation needed on the page. What is used instead is the checkable part: a patent application filed 14 February 2006, and a first-person account from one of its named contributors, Hugh Williams, describing a shipped feature from March 2006, a year before Raskin is generally credited with building his own version at Humanized. This entry does not call Raskin's claim false: both teams may have built something similar within a year of each other, and Raskin's version is simply the one that is popularly credited. The specific, checkable fact used on screen is only that the patent and the primary account both predate the popular attribution. Not claimed: a first-person, dated account from Raskin's side, since one was not found in this pass. The figure beat uses the 1,000 image cap because it directly undercuts the word 'infinite' in the feature's own name.

beats.lead: You've scrolled past this credit a thousand times.
beats.text: The person usually credited with it isn't who built it first.
beats.note: Infinite scroll is one of the most copied interface patterns in software history, and the popular story about its origin is a year off, and about the wrong team.

beats.name: Hugh Williams
beats.role: A Microsoft search engineering lead. He and two colleagues, Julie Farago and Nick Craswell, built the feature into MSN's image search after data showed testers paging through dozens of results rather than stop, one went to around page twenty before clicking a photo of a chocolate cake.

beats.lead: It wasn't just an idea, it was filed.
beats.text: Microsoft's patent for it predates the famous version by a year.
beats.note: Filed 14 February 2006, naming Farago, Williams and a colleague as inventors. The programmer usually credited with inventing infinite scroll built his own version at a different company in 2006, after this one had already shipped.

beats.context: The hard limit Microsoft actually built into its 'infinite' scroll. It was never truly infinite, just longer than anyone expected to reach.

beats.text: The feature everyone recognises. The credit almost nobody has right.

beats.line: Not the founder you've heard of. Three researchers with a data set.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_principle - read in full 1 Sep 2026: Vilfredo Pareto observed in his book Cours d'economie politique that roughly 80% of land in the Kingdom of Italy was owned by about 20% of the population; the article's own citation dates that book to 1896 to 1897, though its prose separately says he 'wrote in 1906'; in 1941, management consultant Joseph M. Juran, having read Pareto's work, generalised the observation and later named it 'the vital few and the useful many'; cites Juran's New York Times obituary (Bunkley, 3 March 2008) for his death at age 103.

https://www.juran.com/blog/a-guide-to-the-pareto-principle-80-20-rule-pareto-analysis/ - read in full 1 Sep 2026, published by the Juran Institute, the company Joseph Juran founded: dates Pareto's original observation to 1895; states Juran 'was the first to point out' that Pareto's finding was a universal principle rather than only an economic one, and separately dates Juran's naming of the phenomenon to 'the early 1950s' rather than 1941; also uses the phrases 'useful many' and 'trivial many' within the same paragraph, rather than treating the kinder phrase as Juran's sole preference.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 1 Sep 2026 against two sources read in full: Wikipedia and the company Juran himself founded. Two conflicts are handled here rather than smoothed over. First, when Pareto made the observation: Wikipedia's own prose says he 'wrote in 1906,' but Wikipedia's own citation dates the source text to 1896 to 1897, and the Juran Institute's site independently gives 1895. 1896 is used in the credit beat as the better source-confirmed date; 1906 looks like it may conflate this with Pareto's separate, later 1906 work. Second, when Juran applied it: Wikipedia, citing Juran's 2008 obituary, says 1941; the Juran Institute's own site instead says the early 1950s. The obituary date is used here as the more specific, dated claim, and this note records the discrepancy rather than hiding it. Also not smoothed over: the Juran Institute's own page uses 'useful many' and 'trivial many' interchangeably, a looser claim than the tidy 'Juran preferred the kinder phrase' framing, so the beats below only use the phrase both sources agree he used, 'vital few.' The figure beat uses Juran's age at death, which does not depend on resolving either date conflict.

beats.lead: You've heard the 80/20 rule treated like a law of nature.
beats.text: It started as one economist's footnote about dirt.
beats.note: In 1896, Vilfredo Pareto noticed that roughly 80 percent of the land in Italy belonged to about 20 percent of the population. That's the whole original observation.

beats.lead: Pareto never called it a rule, a principle, or a law.
beats.text: A different man did that, four decades later.
beats.note: In 1941, engineer Joseph Juran read Pareto's land-ownership statistic and did something Pareto never did: he claimed it was universal, true of defects, sales and complaints, almost anything you can count.

beats.name: Joseph M. Juran
beats.role: An engineer working in quality control. He renamed Pareto's one-off Italian statistic 'the vital few and the useful many,' and spent the following six decades teaching that it applied to almost everything.

beats.context: Juran's age when he died in 2008, having outlived the man he named the principle after by more than eighty years, and taught the idea the whole time.

beats.text: Pareto counted Italian land. Juran turned it into a rule for everything.

beats.line: The 80/20 rule has two authors, and only one gets credited.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_Command - read in full 1 Sep 2026: Atari coin-op president Gene Lipkin saw a radar-screen image in a magazine and told department head Steve Calfee to make a game like it; the loosely defined brief, USSR missiles versus a US defence, went to junior programmer Dave Theurer, fresh off Atari Soccer; the six cities in early versions were named as real California cities, Eureka, San Francisco, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Los Angeles and San Diego; Theurer set two conditions on his own design, that neither attacking nor defending nation be named, and that the player have no way to retaliate, which he considered a scenario of mutual destruction, quoting him: 'I did not want to put the player in a position of being a genocidal maniac. Only a crazy person would sling nuclear weapons without context, right?'; during and after the project Theurer suffered nightmares of nuclear destruction, continuing after release with decreasing regularity (citing Alex Rubens' 2019 book '8-Bit Apocalypse'); the game cannot be won and ends on a screen reading 'THE END' rather than 'Game Over.'

https://barnmegaparsec.blogspot.com/2016/10/dave-theurers-nightmares.html - read in full 1 Sep 2026, secondary corroboration only: independently confirms the six defended cities as real towns on the California coastline, and that the game is structurally unwinnable, quoting the site's own framing: 'You can't win nuclear war.'
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 1 Sep 2026 against the Missile Command Wikipedia article, read in full, which sources Theurer's design choices and nightmares to Alex Rubens' 2019 book '8-Bit Apocalypse: The Untold Story of Atari's Missile Command,' and a 2016 hobbyist blog post read only as secondary corroboration for the city names. Deliberately left out: a widely circulated quote from Theurer about waking in a cold sweat for six months after the project, attributed in several secondary write-ups to a 2013 Polygon feature by the same Alex Rubens. That Polygon page could not be fetched directly in this pass, it returned a blocked-URL error, so the quote and the specific six-month duration are left out rather than repeated from search summaries alone. The safer, source-confirmed claim used instead is Wikipedia's own: the nightmares happened during crunch and continued afterward with decreasing regularity. No figure beat: the strongest available numbers, close to 20,000 cabinets sold, six defended cities, are commercial or mechanical counts rather than the fact the story turns on, so none is enlarged to 300px.

beats.lead: It looks like Cold War propaganda.
beats.text: The designer built it to refuse to be that.
beats.note: Atari's coin-op boss saw a radar-screen photo in a magazine and told his team to make a game like it. The junior programmer he handed it to had other ideas.

beats.name: Dave Theurer
beats.role: A junior programmer, fresh off his first game, Atari Soccer. Given a one-line brief about Soviet missiles and an American defence, he attached two conditions of his own before writing a line of code.

beats.lead: Condition one: no country would ever be named.
beats.text: Condition two: you could never fire back.
beats.note: Theurer refused to give the player a retaliation button. In his own words: 'I did not want to put the player in a position of being a genocidal maniac.' Mutual destruction wasn't a game mechanic to him.

beats.lead: The six cities you're defending were real, at first.
beats.text: Eureka, San Francisco, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Los Angeles, San Diego.
beats.note: The whole California coast, named outright in early versions. Theurer stripped the names before release, leaving the geography to the player's imagination.

beats.lead: As the deadline closed in, the nightmares started.
beats.text: Theurer dreamed about the nuclear blast he was coding.
beats.note: They didn't stop when the game shipped in June 1980, they just came less often. The ending reflects it: the screen doesn't say 'Game Over.' It says 'THE END.' There is no way to win.

beats.line: A missile game with no retaliation button, built by a man who couldn't stop dreaming about it.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_versus_Garry_Kasparov - read in full 1 Sep 2026: Kasparov won the 1996 Philadelphia match 4-2; Deep Blue won the 1997 New York rematch 3.5-2.5, the first defeat of a reigning world chess champion by a computer under standard tournament conditions; Game 1's move 44 was allegedly the result of a bug, in which Deep Blue, unable to settle on a move, resorted to a fail-safe; after losing Game 2 in a position later shown to be drawable, Kasparov accused IBM of cheating, alleging a grandmaster had made moves for the machine, specifically 36.axb5 and 37.Be4; the article's own lead states that although it was reported IBM had dismantled Deep Blue afterward, it in fact remained in operation for several years.

https://theconversation.com/twenty-years-on-from-deep-blue-vs-kasparov-how-a-chess-match-started-the-big-data-revolution-76882 - read in full 1 Sep 2026: academic retrospective corroborating the cheating accusation and IBM's denial (stating the only human intervention was fixing bugs between games); adds that Kasparov's suspicion echoed 18th and 19th century chess-automaton hoaxes; grandmaster John Nunn called one Deep Blue move 'stunning' and 'exceptional'; one of Deep Blue's own designers has said a glitch made the machine pick a move at random rather than its calculated best, which Kasparov read as deeper strategy; the final configuration of the machine controlled 480 custom integrated circuits designed specifically to play chess; IBM refused Kasparov's request for a rematch.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 1 Sep 2026 against two sources read in full: Wikipedia's 'Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov' and The Conversation's twenty-years-on retrospective. Both agree on the core shape: Kasparov lost the 1997 rematch, accused IBM of secret human intervention, and IBM denied it. Two points are handled rather than smoothed over. First, which game held the fail-safe bug: Wikipedia specifically places it in Game 1, move 44, a game Deep Blue lost. The Conversation's account of a glitch causing a random move is worded more loosely, and its surrounding context reads as though it may describe Game 2 instead. Rather than assign a game number only one source clearly supports, the bug beat here states only what both sources agree on in substance, a bug produced an unplanned move Kasparov misread as strategic depth, without naming a game. Second, Deep Blue's fate after the match: Wikipedia's lead explicitly corrects a popular report that IBM dismantled the machine, saying it remained in operation for several years; The Conversation instead refers in passing to 'the subsequent dismantling of Deep Blue' as settled fact. Given that direct contradiction, neither version is asserted on screen; the entry uses only what both sources support without conflict, that no rematch ever took place. No figure beat drawn from the match score or the disputed move numbers, both address-style numbers per the style guide; 480, the number of custom chess chips in the machine, is used instead because it is a whole, source-confirmed number that explains the mechanism of the win rather than just labelling it.

beats.lead: Kasparov lost, and said it wasn't fair.
beats.text: He accused IBM of secretly using a human grandmaster.
beats.note: After Deep Blue beat the reigning world chess champion in 1997, Garry Kasparov refused to believe a machine had done it. It echoed 18th and 19th century chess-automaton hoaxes, in which a hidden person, not the machine, did the actual playing.

beats.lead: His evidence was two suspiciously good moves.
beats.text: Moves 36 and 37 in one game looked too human to be brute force.
beats.note: Kasparov and grandmaster observers felt the moves were too sophisticated for a machine playing by raw calculation. IBM denied any human intervention beyond fixing bugs between games.

beats.lead: One of those bugs is real, and documented.
beats.text: A glitch made Deep Blue pick a move at random rather than its best-calculated one.
beats.note: One of the machine's own designers has said a fail-safe kicked in when the computer couldn't settle on a move, and Kasparov read the random result as a sign of deeper strategy than was actually there.

beats.context: Custom chess-only processors built into the machine, working in parallel. Not learning, not intuition, just purpose-built calculation at scale.

beats.lead: Kasparov spent years demanding a rematch.
beats.text: IBM never gave him one.
beats.note: Deep Blue's exact fate after 1997 is described differently by different accounts, but every account agrees on this: the third match Kasparov wanted never happened.

beats.line: A grudge that has outlasted the hardware it was about.

sources: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/great-wall-of-china-from-space/ - read in full 1 Sep 2026 (Mara Hvistendahl, 21 Feb 2008): the myth that the Great Wall is visible from space predates spaceflight, tracing to a 1932 Ripley's Believe It or Not cartoon, three decades before Yuri Gagarin's first orbital flight; Apollo astronauts including Neil Armstrong stated no human structures are visible from the Moon; NASA oral histories quote Shuttle astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman saying he never saw the Great Wall from orbit; NASA's own published assessment is that the wall is barely visible even from 180 miles up and is comparable in width to a highway.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2003/10/17/chinas-spaceman-shatters-a-myth - read in full 1 Sep 2026: contemporaneous report on Yang Liwei, China's first astronaut, completing 14 orbits aboard Shenzhou 5 in October 2003 and telling reporters on his return that the scenery was beautiful but he didn't see the Great Wall, directly puncturing the myth for a domestic Chinese audience; reports that China's Ministry of Education subsequently corrected an elementary-school textbook that had stated the wall was visible from space.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 1 Sep 2026 against two sources read in full, a Scientific American explainer citing NASA astronauts directly, and an Al Jazeera news report on Yang Liwei's 2003 flight. Both independently support the structure used here: the myth predates spaceflight itself, since the 1932 Ripley's cartoon came decades before anyone had actually been to orbit, and it has since been directly denied by astronauts from both the American and Chinese space programmes. The wall's width, roughly six metres, narrower than most two-lane roads, is used as the figure beat because it is the specific physical reason a many-thousand-kilometre structure still isn't visible to the naked eye: width, not length, is what naked-eye resolution from orbit depends on. Not claimed: a single precise average width figure beyond 'roughly six metres,' since the wall's width varies considerably along its length and by the dynasty that built each section, and neither source gives one exact average.

beats.lead: It's the one 'fact' every schoolkid knows.
beats.text: The Great Wall of China is visible from space.
beats.note: It's repeated so often it feels like common knowledge. It has never been true, and how the claim got started is stranger than the myth itself.

beats.lead: The claim predates the Space Age by nearly thirty years.
beats.text: It comes from a 1932 Ripley's Believe It or Not cartoon.
beats.note: Nobody had been to space yet. The claim wasn't a report of what someone saw, it was a guess, printed as fact, decades before Yuri Gagarin's first orbital flight in 1961.

beats.name: Yang Liwei
beats.role: China's first astronaut. After 14 orbits aboard Shenzhou 5, he came back down and told reporters the scenery was beautiful, but he hadn't seen the Great Wall. China's own education ministry then corrected a textbook that had taught the myth as fact.

beats.lead: American astronauts had already said the same thing.
beats.text: Apollo's Neil Armstrong said no human structures are visible from the Moon.
beats.note: Shuttle astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman put it plainly: he never saw the Great Wall. From low orbit, under near-perfect light, the wall is sometimes barely visible, and easily mistaken for an ordinary road.

beats.context: Roughly how wide the wall is. A structure can stretch for thousands of kilometres and still be invisible from orbit if it's no wider than a road, length was never the problem.

beats.line: Wrong since before anyone could check, and repeated ever since.

Established the 1955 proposal text quoted directly (a '2 month, 10 man study'), that John McCarthy coined the term 'artificial intelligence' in that document and chose it partly to avoid 'cybernetics' and Norbert Wiener, that the workshop ran roughly eight weeks (about 18 June to 17 August 1956) by Ray Solomonoff's own contemporaneous notes though it is usually said to be six weeks, that only McCarthy, Marvin Minsky and Solomonoff stayed the full time, and that daily attendance ranged from about three to eight people.

https://spectrum.ieee.org/dartmouth-ai-workshop: Grace Solomonoff, IEEE Spectrum, read in full. Confirmed the exact dates (18 June to 17 August 1956), established that Herbert Simon and Allen Newell presented the Logic Theory Machine that summer and later won the 1975 Turing Award for the ideas behind it, and that in 2006 Trenchard More located the same dictionary the group had used to look up 'heuristic', still in the room where the workshop was held.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 3 Sep 2026. No figure beat used for a funding amount: neither source gave a confirmed Rockefeller Foundation grant figure, so none is claimed. Not stated as fact that this was the first ever meeting on the subject: the Dartmouth Wikipedia page itself notes it followed the 1951 Paris cybernetics conference and the Macy conferences, so the sign line is about the name the field got here, not about a first gathering. The three to eight person attendance range is Wikipedia's own citation to Nilsson's history of AI, read as presented in the Wikipedia text rather than in the book itself.

beats.lead: AI is always said to have begun with a landmark meeting of minds
beats.text: Most days, three to eight people actually showed up.
beats.note: The 1955 proposal asked the Rockefeller Foundation to fund '10 men' for '2 months'. Only three of them, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky and Ray Solomonoff, stayed for the entire eight weeks.

beats.name: John McCarthy
beats.role: Wrote the funding proposal with Minsky, Rochester and Shannon, and coined the field's name inside it. He wanted a neutral term, anything but 'cybernetics', which would have meant working under the combative Norbert Wiener.

beats.lead: One talk that summer outlasted the rest
beats.text: Newell and Simon showed a program that already reasoned.
beats.note: Their Logic Theory Machine used symbolic logic to prove mathematical theorems. In 1975 they won computing's highest honour, the Turing Award, for the work it began.

beats.context: How long the workshop actually ran, from 18 June to 17 August 1956, by the attendees' own notes. It is usually remembered as six.

beats.text: The dictionary they used to look up 'heuristic' is still in that room.

beats.line: Three people. Eight weeks. One new field.

No figure beat used for the damage range itself (263 to 337), since a range is not a single defensible number; the 30 second kill time is the clean figure both sources state directly. Not claimed: a specific patient zero. Wikipedia states no index case was ever identified, and PC Gamer only narrows it to the Archimonde server without naming an individual, so no beat claims to know who started the spread. Subscriber and revenue figures for World of Warcraft at the time were read but left out, since they describe the game's popularity generally rather than this incident.

beats.lead: It is often remembered as one of Blizzard's cleverest ideas
beats.text: It was actually one missing line of code.
beats.note: A raid boss called Hakkar cast a debuff meant to stay inside a single zone. Developers forgot to clear it from players' pets when a fight ended, so infected pets carried it straight into crowded cities.

beats.lead: Blizzard's own engineers did not understand it either, at first
beats.text: 'It was really scary when we didn't know why it was happening.'
beats.note: Lead engineer John Cash, describing the week it took just to diagnose the bug. The eventual fix reset every server back to before the outbreak began.

beats.context: How fast the debuff alone could kill the game's highest level characters. There was no cure inside the game, only distance.

beats.name: Lofgren and Fefferman
beats.role: Epidemiologists who published the outbreak in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, arguing that a buggy video game had modelled real human panic, self quarantine and reckless spreading better than any deliberate simulation could.

beats.text: The CDC called. Blizzard told them it was just a bug.

beats.line: Real players. Fake blood. Real epidemiology.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emu_War: read in full. Established the operational chronology (2 November 1932 first engagement, 4 November dam ambush where a Lewis gun jammed after 12 confirmed kills, 8 November withdrawal after 2,500 rounds fired, resumption on 13 November, recall on 10 December), Major G.P.W. Meredith's command of two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds, his report claiming 986 confirmed kills from 9,860 rounds fired (a rate of exactly 10 rounds per kill, which historian Greg Beyer calls likely inflated), the roughly 20,000 emus that had moved onto Wheatbelt farmland, and the 1923 bounty scheme under which 57,034 bounties were claimed in six months of 1934, far exceeding the military operation's result.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 3 Sep 2026. Single source, but the Wikipedia article is itself built largely from directly quoted 1932 newspaper reporting (The Argus, the Canberra Times, the Coolgardie Miner) and a peer reviewed history (Johnson, 2006, Journal of Australian Studies), all read within the article text. Attempts to reach a second outlet directly (Smithsonian Magazine, the Australian War Memorial, Trove's own newspaper archive) either redirected to an unrelated article or blocked automated access, so this entry stands on one thoroughly cited source rather than two independently read ones, flagged here rather than hidden. The figure beat uses the bounty count rather than Meredith's own kill claim, since the bounty number is not disputed by historians the way his report's total is. Not claimed: any single 'total emus killed' figure for the military operation, since the sources give a range for the first phase alone and Meredith's later total is explicitly called inflated.

beats.lead: The popular version says Australia lost a war to emus
beats.text: It was not a war. It was pest control that went badly.
beats.note: In November 1932 farmers in Western Australia's Wheatbelt asked for army machine guns against emus ruining their wheat. What followed looked far less organised than the name suggests.

beats.name: Major G.P.W. Meredith
beats.role: Royal Australian Artillery. Commanded two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition against roughly 20,000 emus that had moved onto farmland, a target that would not hold still to be shot at.

beats.lead: The clearest ambush of the campaign still went wrong
beats.text: Over 1,000 emus approached. The gun jammed after 12 were hit.
beats.note: Near a dam on 4 November, Meredith's men waited for the flock to come close before opening fire. One Lewis gun seized almost at once and the rest of the birds scattered.

beats.context: Claimed by ordinary bounty hunters in just six months of 1934, under a scheme that had existed since 1923, far more than Meredith's whole campaign managed with soldiers and machine guns.

beats.text: Paperwork did what the machine guns could not.

beats.line: Not really a war. Just extremely persistent birds.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorne_effect: read in full. French coined the term 'Hawthorne effect' in 1953, that economists Steven Levitt and John List located the original illumination data on microfilm at the University of Wisconsin in Milwaukee in 2011 and published a reanalysis finding only slight, not drastic, evidence for the effect, that this matched an earlier 1992 reanalysis by S. R. G. Jones, and Richard Nisbett's quoted description of the effect as 'a glorified anecdote'.

topics.verifiedNote: Checked 3 Sep 2026. Deliberately not claimed: that the Hawthorne effect is false or fully debunked. Levitt and List reported 'slight evidence, in no way as drastic as suggested initially', not zero evidence, and List is quoted saying he still believes the effect is genuine, so the beats say the evidence is weak and disputed rather than disproven. beats.lead: Every management course teaches the Hawthorne effect
beats.text: People supposedly work harder simply because they know they are being watched.
beats.note: That lesson comes from a 1920s factory study. There is a problem: the economists who finally found the original data were not convinced it happened as taught.

beats.name: John R. P. French
beats.role: Coined the term 'Hawthorne effect', nearly three decades after the studies it describes had ended. The name was applied retrospectively to results nobody had cleanly explained at the time.

beats.lead: The original lighting study gave itself away
beats.text: Output rose in the room where nothing changed too.
beats.note: Researchers dimmed and brightened the lights in one room while leaving a second, unlit control room alone. Productivity climbed in both, which meant the lighting was never the real variable.

beats.context: How long the original 1924 lighting data sat unexamined, until economists Steven Levitt and John List found it on microfilm in 2011 and reported only weak support for the effect nearly everyone had been taught.

beats.lead: One psychologist put it more bluntly
beats.text: 'A glorified anecdote.'
beats.note: Richard Nisbett's verdict on the whole idea: 'Once you have got the anecdote, you can throw away the data.'

beats.line: The most cited finding in management may itself be a myth.

topics.verifiedNote: Checked 3 Sep 2026. Deliberately not stated as settled: the exact terms of the Thermo Fisher or Novartis settlements, since both are reported as undisclosed. Deliberately not stated: that the Ultragenyx or Viatris lawsuits have concluded, since the source marks them as still pending as of March 2026. beats.lead: The Henrietta Lacks story usually ends on an injustice with no resolution
beats.text: It is now also a story about lawsuits actually being won.
beats.note: In 2021 her estate sued the companies that had profited for decades from her cells. Thermo Fisher Scientific settled in 2023. Novartis followed in 2026.

beats.name: Henrietta Lacks
beats.role: A 31 year old mother of five, treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital. Doctors took a tissue sample during her biopsy without telling her. She died the same year.

beats.lead: Every sample taken before hers had died within days
beats.text: Hers doubled every 20 to 24 hours, and simply did not stop.
beats.note: Cell biologist George Gey's lab had collected samples from cancer patients for years. Lacks's were the first that would not die in a dish, the first human cell line to survive indefinitely outside a body.

beats.context: The count of scientific papers built on HeLa cells by 2009 alone, and still climbing then by more than 300 a month.

beats.lead: Those cells eventually solved their own origin story
beats.text: In the 1980s, a scientist found the virus that had caused her cancer, still living in her cells.
beats.note: Harald zur Hausen identified HPV18 in the original HeLa sample, the same virus that had caused Lacks's cervical cancer. The discovery won him a Nobel Prize and led directly to the HPV vaccine.

beats.line: Her cells have outlived her by three quarters of a century, and are still dividing.

beats.lead: Every New Year's, someone points out that Y2K was nothing
beats.text: It was nothing because thousands of programmers spent years making sure of it
beats.note: Two-digit year fields, standard practice in software written from the 1960s onward to save expensive memory, would have read '00' as 1900 once 1999 ticked over, breaking date maths across banking, aviation and power systems worldwide.

beats.name: John Koskinen
beats.role: Appointed by President Clinton to chair the President's Council on Year 2000 Conversion, reporting directly to the White House and coordinating the fix across every federal agency.

beats.text: They still run from about $100 billion to $600 billion

sources: https://courses.cs.umbc.edu/471/papers/turing.pdf — Turing's original 1950 paper, Mind 49: 433-460, read in full. topics.verifiedNote: Checked 4 Sep 2026. No figure beat: nothing in the paper or its history offered a number worth putting at 300px. 1950 is a date, already carried by the credit beat, and a duration (years between the paper and Turing's death, or between the paper and the name catching on) is not a claim that carries the story on its own, the same reasoning great-emu-war used to cut a duration figure. Dropped entirely: a claim that Weizenbaum's 1966 CACM paper on ELIZA used the phrase 'Turing's test'. It shows up in secondary summaries but I could not find the actual sentence in a source I read directly, so it is left unclaimed rather than asserted on a paraphrase of a paraphrase. Not claimed: who specifically coined the phrase 'the Turing test' or exactly when; the sources describe the renaming as posthumous and gradual, not a single event, so the beats say only that Turing himself never used the phrase and that it came later.

beats.lead: The Turing Test sounds like a machine trying to pass for a person
beats.text: Turing never called it that, and it didn't start with a machine at all
beats.note: His 1950 paper names it 'the imitation game': a man and a woman try to convince an interrogator, using written notes alone, which of them is which.

beats.lead: The man's task in that first version was oddly specific
beats.text: Convince the interrogator that he was the woman
beats.note: Turing's own sample question to the players was about hair length. Only after laying out that contest does he ask what happens if a machine takes the man's place, and whether it fools people just as often.

beats.name: Alan Turing
beats.role: Published 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' in the journal Mind, opening not with a definition of thinking but with a parlour game about gender and deception.

beats.text: He died in 1954. The name arrived afterwards, and without him.

beats.line: The game on paper and the test everyone quotes are not quite the same game.

topics.verifiedNote: Checked 4 Sep 2026. beats.lead: IBM's Watson had just spent five years learning to answer like a person
beats.text: Its most famous answer on air was five question marks of doubt
beats.note: Final Jeopardy!, category US Cities: its largest airport named for a World War II hero, its second largest for a World War II battle. The answer was Chicago. Watson buzzed in with 'What is Toronto?????'

beats.lead: Toronto was not a wild guess
beats.text: Watson rated it 14% likely, Chicago only 11%
beats.note: Its confidence in either answer was too low to trust, and Toronto had two things working for it: a small Illinois town with the same name, and a Canadian baseball team playing in the American League.

beats.name: David Ferrucci
beats.role: Led the IBM research team that spent five years building Watson's DeepQA system, kept offline throughout, to compete on the hardest quiz show on television.

beats.context: More than triple what either human champion won on their own. IBM donated the entire amount to charity.

beats.text: An IBM engineer wore a Toronto Blue Jays jacket to the next day's taping.

beats.line: The machine that won still hedged out loud when it wasn't sure.

beats.lead: Esports is usually dated to the 2000s, LAN parties and stadiums
beats.text: The earliest tournament on record ran in a Stanford computer lab in 1972
beats.note: The Intergalactic Spacewar Olympics, organised by Rolling Stone writer Stewart Brand, took place on the evening of 19 October 1972 at Stanford's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, with roughly twenty competitors.

beats.name: Bruce Baumgart
beats.role: A Stanford graduate student who won the five-player free-for-all, practising left-handed and two-fisted play against beginners just to keep his own games interesting.

beats.lead: First prize was not exactly a career-changer
beats.text: A year of Rolling Stone magazine, and by one attendee's account, some beer
beats.note: Stewart Brand organised the tournament and covered it himself for a Rolling Stone feature, 'Fanatic Life and Symbolic Death Among the Computer Bums', published 7 December 1972.

beats.lead: The senator who forced the games industry to rate itself was working from a description, not the game
beats.text: He said women were hung on meat hooks and drained into wine bottles. Neither was in it.
beats.note: On 9 December 1993, Senator Joseph Lieberman, joined by Herbert Kohl and Byron Dorgan, held hearings condemning the Sega CD game Night Trap using details that were not actually part of its plot.

beats.role: Senator for Connecticut. Opened a press conference on 1 December 1993 denouncing 'violent video games', flanked by the National PTA and former Captain Kangaroo star Bob Keeshan, then led the December hearings naming Mortal Kombat and Night Trap directly.

beats.lead: The industry's own witnesses did not present a united front
beats.text: Nintendo and Sega mostly used the hearing to blame each other

beats.line: One misdescribed game is why every game box has a rating on it.

sources: https://deepseanews.com/2013/07/are-jellyfish-immortal/ — RR Helm, a jellyfish biologist, read in full. Cites and summarises Piraino, Boero, Aeschbach and Schmid (1996), 'Reversing the Life Cycle: Medusae Transforming into Polyps and Cell Transdifferentiation in Turritopsis nutricula (Cnidaria, Hydrozoa)', Biological Bulletin 190(3):302-312, the paper documenting the species (now Turritopsis dohrnii) reverting from an injured or ageing medusa back into the earlier polyp stage via transdifferentiation. topics.verifiedNote: Checked 5 Sep 2026. The nickname is real and the mechanism behind it is real and published, but the word immortal is doing more work than the science supports, and the article's own author, a working jellyfish biologist, says so directly: I'm not convinced. What is documented is transdifferentiation, a stressed or damaged medusa reverting to the polyp stage instead of dying, not a demonstrated absence of ageing. The aquarist testimony is the actual evidence used here: colonies maintained for roughly six years get measurably worse, which reads like senescence at the colony level even if a single polyp's fate is harder to track. No figure beat: the six year figure is anecdotal aquarist experience, not a measured study result, so it is used as spoken texture rather than a rendered statistic. Deliberately not claimed: that any individual has been shown to cycle indefinitely, or a count of how often reversal happens in the wild. The phenomenon is documented in the lab and by aquarists, not tracked across a wild population.

beats.lead: The internet's favourite immortality story
beats.text: It cheats death. It does not skip ageing.
beats.note: Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from an adult jellyfish back into its earlier polyp stage when it is stressed, injured, or ageing. That part is real and published.

beats.name: Stefano Piraino and team
beats.role: Described the reversal in the Biological Bulletin, using the phrase escaping death and achieving potential immortality, a title that outran the caveats inside its own paper.

beats.lead: Ask the people who actually keep them
beats.text: Their colonies still get old.
beats.note: Aquarists who maintain polyp stock for years report it turning fragile after about six years: fewer healthy jellies, weaker responses. Reversing a life stage is not the same as not ageing.

beats.text: Even the biologist who wrote it up says: I'm not convinced.

beats.line: A trick for surviving one bad day. Not a loophole in death.

sources: https://neuroscience.stanford.edu/news/your-gut-second-brain — Stanford's Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute, read in full, article plus full podcast transcript with Dr Julia Kaltschmidt. Establishes 100 to 600 million neurons in the human gut's enteric nervous system, run in two neural sheets from the oesophagus to the rectum; that this is more neurons than the spinal cord contains; that it uses more than 30 different neurotransmitters, the same signalling chemicals as the brain; that it can function with no connection to the brain at all, since an isolated mouse gut in a dish still shows coordinated activity; that it does not generate conscious thought; and that the term second brain was coined in 1996 by Columbia gastroenterologist Michael Gershon, author of the book of the same name.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 5 Sep 2026. The comparison on screen is Stanford's own: 100 to 600 million neurons is about as many as you'd find in the brain of a fruit bat, an ostrich, or a Yorkshire Terrier. No figure beat: Stanford states the count as a range, not a settled number, and rendering one end of a 100 to 600 million range as a giant precise digit would claim more certainty than the source does, so the range is spoken instead. What the beats do not claim: that the gut thinks, decides, or feels in the way the phrase second brain implies day to day. Kaltschmidt is explicit that it does not generate conscious thought. The correction this video makes is that second brain is a real, technical claim about an autonomous, neuron-dense nervous system, not a poetic one about a second mind.

beats.lead: You have heard your gut called a second brain
beats.text: That is not a figure of speech.
beats.note: The lining of your gut holds a real, dense network of neurons, running from your oesophagus to your rectum, with its own name: the enteric nervous system.

beats.name: Michael Gershon
beats.role: Columbia gastroenterologist who coined the term second brain and wrote the book on it, arguing the gut's nervous system deserved to be studied as more than plumbing.

beats.lead: What makes it earn the name
beats.text: It can run with the brain disconnected.
beats.note: It has more neurons than your spinal cord, uses over thirty of the same signalling chemicals as your brain, and keeps working in a gut removed entirely from the body.

beats.text: It cannot think for you. It can absolutely talk to you.

beats.line: Gut instinct has more nerve behind it than the phrase lets on.

sources: https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/saturn-could-float-on-water — BBC Sky at Night Magazine, read in full.
